bansda-state.t: A Solanki Rajput state in the forested hills of southern Gujarat, beside the Dangs.
bansda-state.o: The rulers of Vansda (Bansda) were Solanki Rajputs whose line claimed descent from the Chaulukya kings of Gujarat. Their small hill state emerged as a distinct principality in the 18th century and came under Maratha and then British supervision.
bansda-state.r: Bansda was a 9-gun salute state of the Surat Agency, later the Gujarat States Agency, governed by a Maharawal over a forested, largely Adivasi territory of Kokna, Bhil and other communities. Timber and forest produce were the main resources.
bansda-state.e: After accession to India Bansda was merged into Bombay State in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. Its former forests are protected in the Vansda National Park in Navsari district.

breuci.t: Pannonian people of the lower Sava valley who led, and then betrayed, the great revolt against Rome of 6–9 CE.
breuci.o: The Breuci lived along the lower Sava in modern Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia, among the Pannonian peoples of the region. They appear in Roman sources from the 2nd century BCE, when Roman armies first pushed into the Sava valley.
breuci.r: Known mainly from Roman accounts, they were a populous tribal people of farmers and stockbreeders, said to field large armies. In 6 CE, when Rome levied troops for a war against the Marcomanni, they rose under Bato the Breucian and Pinnes, joining the Daesitiates in the Great Illyrian Revolt.
breuci.e: In 8 CE Bato the Breucian surrendered Pinnes to Rome and was then executed by Bato of the Daesitiates. The Breuci submitted, and their young men were enrolled in Roman auxiliary units, the cohortes Breucorum, that served across the empire.

baekje.t: A southwestern Korean kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, celebrated for refined Buddhist art and for passing writing and Buddhism to Japan.
baekje.o: Tradition holds that Onjo, a son of Goguryeo's founder, established Baekje in 18 BCE at Wiryeseong on the Han river. It began as one statelet of the Mahan confederacy and grew to dominate it, reaching its peak under King Geunchogo, who killed a Goguryeo king in battle in 371.
baekje.r: An aristocracy of leading clans served kings who traced descent from Buyeo. Buddhism arrived in 384. Driven south by Goguryeo in 475, the court moved to Ungjin (Gongju) and in 538 to Sabi. Baekje traded with southern Chinese dynasties and maintained close ties to Yamato, sending scholars, artisans and Buddhist images; the gilt-bronze incense burner and King Muryeong's tomb show its craftsmanship.
baekje.e: King Seong was killed fighting Silla in 554. In 660 a Silla and Tang alliance took Sabi and King Uija surrendered. A restoration movement backed by Yamato was crushed at Baekgang in 663, and many refugees settled in Japan.

bahia-republic.t: The Sabinada, a revolt that proclaimed a republic in Salvador in 1837 until the young Emperor Pedro II came of age, crushed within four months.
bahia-republic.o: During the unstable regency period in the Empire of Brazil, discontent in Salvador over central control and military recruitment for the war in Rio Grande do Sul came to a head. On 7 November 1837 rebels led by the doctor Francisco Sabino Vieira took the city and proclaimed the Bahia Republic.
bahia-republic.r: The revolt was led by urban professionals, officers and soldiers. Its leaders declared Bahia independent only until Pedro II reached adulthood, a compromise reflecting divisions among them. They offered freedom to Brazilian-born enslaved people who fought for the republic. The rebels never controlled the Recôncavo sugar region, whose planters supported the imperial government.
bahia-republic.e: Imperial forces besieged Salvador by land and sea and retook it in March 1838 after fierce street fighting with heavy loss of life. Sabino was exiled to Mato Grosso, and the revolt became known as the Sabinada after him.

blue-horde.t: The western wing of the Golden Horde, the realm of Batu and his heirs on the Volga, Don and Dnieper steppes.
blue-horde.o: After the conquest of the western steppe and Rus' between 1236 and 1242, the Jochid lands were divided into two wings. The western or right wing, ruled by Batu from Sarai on the lower Volga, is often called the Blue Horde, though medieval sources use the colour names inconsistently.
blue-horde.r: The western wing was the core of the Golden Horde, controlling the Rus' principalities, the Volga trade and the Crimean ports. Its khans, including Berke, Uzbek Khan and Jani Beg, held authority over the whole Jochid realm. Under its rule Islam spread among the elite and Sarai grew into a major trading city.
blue-horde.e: After Jani Beg's murder in 1357, decades of civil war followed, and in 1378 the White Horde khan Tokhtamysh seized Sarai and reunited the two wings. The western lands later broke into the Khanate of Kazan, the Crimean Khanate, the Astrakhan Khanate and the Great Horde.

baroda-state.t: The Maratha kingdom of the Gaekwads in Gujarat, one of the richest princely states and, under Sayajirao III, a pioneer of free schooling and public libraries.
baroda-state.o: Pilaji Rao Gaekwad, a commander serving the Dabhade family and the Maratha state, seized Songadh in 1721 and used it as a base for raids into Mughal Gujarat. His son Damaji Rao II took Baroda (Vadodara) and much of the province, and the Gaekwads became one of the great Maratha houses alongside the Peshwas, Holkars and Scindias.
baroda-state.r: After disputed successions, Baroda entered a subsidiary alliance with the East India Company in 1802–05. In 1875 the British deposed Malhar Rao for an alleged attempt to poison the Resident. His adopted successor Sayajirao Gaekwad III (1875–1939) introduced compulsory primary education, a state library network, courts and railways, banned child marriage and funded scholars including B. R. Ambedkar. The state ranked among the few with a 21-gun salute.
baroda-state.e: Pratapsinh Gaekwad acceded to India in 1947, and on 1 May 1949 Baroda was merged into Bombay State; since 1960 it has been part of Gujarat. The Lakshmi Vilas Palace and the Maharaja Sayajirao University are its best-known legacies.

bhavnagar-state.t: The Gohil Rajput port state of eastern Kathiawar whose last ruler was the first prince to hand his state over to the Indian people.
bhavnagar-state.o: The Gohil Rajputs had ruled in southern Saurashtra since the 13th century from Sihor. In 1723 Bhavsinhji I founded the port of Bhavnagar on the Gulf of Khambhat and moved his capital there, giving the state its name. It was also known as Gohilwad after the ruling clan.
bhavnagar-state.r: Bhavnagar grew rich from sea trade, especially cotton exported to Bombay, and cooperated with the British against piracy in the Gulf. Under rulers such as Takhtsinhji it built railways, colleges and hospitals and was regarded as one of the better-administered states of the Kathiawar Agency, with Prabhashankar Pattani as a noted diwan.
bhavnagar-state.e: In January 1948 Krishnakumarsinhji announced the transfer of power to a popular government, and Bhavnagar was merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948; it has been in Gujarat since 1960. Krishnakumarsinhji later served as Governor of Madras.

barbados.t: Easternmost Caribbean island, independent since 1966 and a parliamentary republic since 2021, with one of the region's oldest parliaments.
barbados.o: English settlers arrived in 1627, and Barbados became the first great sugar and slave society of the English Caribbean, with a House of Assembly dating from 1639. After labour riots in 1937 and the rise of Grantley Adams's Barbados Labour Party, it achieved self-government, and under Errol Barrow of the Democratic Labour Party it became independent on 30 November 1966.
barbados.r: For 55 years Barbados was a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Power alternated peacefully between the Democratic Labour Party and the Barbados Labour Party. Barrow and Tom Adams invested in education and health, and the economy shifted from sugar to tourism and offshore financial services, giving the island one of the highest living standards in the region.
barbados.e: On 30 November 2021 Barbados became a parliamentary republic, with Sandra Mason as the first president and the singer Rihanna named a national hero. Prime Minister Mia Mottley, in office since 2018, has promoted the Bridgetown Initiative on climate finance.

bijna-state.t: A tiny chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency, one of the smallest polities recognised by the British in central India.
bijna-state.o: Bijna was recognised as a separate holding under British protection in the early 19th century, one of a number of small Bundela estates confirmed after the British gained supremacy in Bundelkhand.
bijna-state.r: Little is recorded of its history; it consisted of a few villages under a hereditary chief supervised by the political agent in Bundelkhand.
bijna-state.e: After independence Bijna was merged into Vindhya Pradesh with the other Bundelkhand states, and its lands were absorbed into the Indian administration by 1950.

bihwa-gaya.t: A Gaya statelet at Changnyeong on the Nakdong river, the first of the Gaya polities to fall under Silla's sway.
bihwa-gaya.o: Bihwa Gaya, called Bisabeol in Silla records, developed from a Byeonhan-era community in the Changnyeong basin on the east bank of the Nakdong. Its large mounded tombs at Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong date mainly from the 5th century.
bihwa-gaya.r: Little is recorded of its rulers. The tomb goods, including gilt-bronze crowns and stoneware in Silla style, show that the local elite was drawn into Silla's orbit early while keeping its own burial grounds, and the polity served as a gateway between Silla and the western Gaya states.
bihwa-gaya.e: Silla established a province at Bisabeol in 555 and King Jinheung erected a stele there in 561 recording his tour and naming his officials, marking the area's full incorporation. The tombs of Songhyeon-dong yielded a well-preserved sacrificed girl, reconstructed in 2008.

bechuanaland-protectorate.t: The British protectorate over the Tswana kingdoms, ruled from outside its own borders, which became independent Botswana.
bechuanaland-protectorate.o: Britain declared a protectorate over the land north of the Molopo River in 1885, after the Warren Expedition, to block German and Boer expansion and keep open the road to the interior. Tswana rulers such as Khama III of the Bangwato Kingdom welcomed protection against the Boers and the Ndebele.
bechuanaland-protectorate.r: Administration was minimal and ran from Mafeking, outside the territory. In 1895 Khama III, Sebele and Bathoen travelled to London and persuaded the government not to hand them to Cecil Rhodes's company. Chiefs kept wide powers, and many men worked in South African mines. The marriage of Seretse Khama to a white Englishwoman in 1948 led Britain to exile him under South African pressure.
bechuanaland-protectorate.e: Seretse Khama returned to lead the Bechuanaland Democratic Party, which won the 1965 election. The territory became independent as Botswana on 30 September 1966, with a new capital at Gaborone and Seretse Khama as president.

belgae-britain.t: Central southern British people around Winchester, whose name recalls the Belgae of northern Gaul and who formed a civitas of Roman Britain.
belgae-britain.o: Caesar wrote that the coastal parts of Britain had been settled by Belgae from Gaul who kept their tribal names, and Belgic coins circulated widely in the south from the 2nd century BCE. A people called Belgae is named only from Roman times, however, and their pre-conquest identity is uncertain; Winchester, the later Venta Belgarum, had a late Iron Age enclosure at Oram's Arbour.
belgae-britain.r: Before the conquest the region of Hampshire and Wiltshire seems to have fallen within the sphere of the Atrebates (Britain) and their kings Commius, Tincomarus and Verica, sharing their coinage and links with Gaul. Farming was rich on the chalk downs, and hillforts such as Danebury had been major storage centres in earlier centuries.
belgae-britain.e: After 43 the area may first have been part of the realm of Togidubnus in the Kingdom of the Regni. On his death it was organised as the civitas of the Belgae, with Venta Belgarum as its capital; Ptolemy also lists Aquae Sulis, Bath, among their towns. Winchester later became the royal seat of Wessex.

bremen-verden.t: Two secularised prince-bishoprics between the Elbe and Weser that Sweden ruled as duchies from 1648 until losing them to Denmark and Hanover.
bremen-verden.o: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 turned the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen and the Prince-Bishopric of Verden into secular duchies and granted them to Sweden as imperial fiefs. The Swedish crown thus gained a seat in the Imperial Diet and control of the mouths of the Elbe and Weser.
bremen-verden.r: Sweden governed the duchies from Stade, which it fortified, through a governor-general and the local estates. The city of Bremen claimed to be a free imperial city, and Sweden fought two wars against it in 1654 and 1666 without subduing it. The lands were mainly marsh and heath farming country with a Lutheran population.
bremen-verden.e: During the Great Northern War Denmark occupied the duchies in 1712. Denmark sold them in 1715 to the Electorate of Hanover, whose elector was also George I of Great Britain, and Sweden ceded them formally in 1719. They later formed part of Hanover and of the German state of Lower Saxony.

bonapartist-spain.t: The Spanish kingdom of Joseph Bonaparte, imposed by Napoleon in 1808 and swept away by the Peninsular War.
bonapartist-spain.o: In 1808 Napoleon summoned Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII to Bayonne and forced both to abdicate. He gave the throne to his brother Joseph, who was proclaimed Joseph I and granted the Statute of Bayonne, Spain's first constitution, while the Madrid rising of 2 May was brutally suppressed.
bonapartist-spain.r: Joseph's government, supported by reformist afrancesados, abolished the Inquisition, seigneurial rights and many convents. But it depended entirely on French armies and never controlled the whole country. Patriot juntas, the Cortes of Cádiz with its Constitution of 1812, guerrillas and Wellington's Anglo-Portuguese army fought it throughout the Peninsular War.
bonapartist-spain.e: After the defeat at Vitoria in June 1813 Joseph left Spain. By the Treaty of Valençay in December 1813 Napoleon restored Ferdinand VII, returning the country to Bourbon Spain.

barony-of-akova.t: Frankish barony in the hills of western Arcadia, centred on the castle the French called Matagrifon, lost to the Byzantines in 1320.
barony-of-akova.o: The barony of Akova was among the twelve original baronies of the Principality of Achaea, created around 1209 and granted to Walter of Rosieres, with 24 knight's fiefs. Its castle in the mountains between Elis and Arcadia was called Matagrifon, 'kill the Greeks', reflecting its role in holding down the region.
barony-of-akova.r: The barons owed service to the prince and sat in his high court. After the Rosieres line died out, the inheritance of Margaret of Passavant to Akova was disputed in the 1270s, a famous case recorded in the Chronicle of the Morea and in the Assizes of Romania, and much of the barony passed to the princely domain.
barony-of-akova.e: In 1320 the Byzantine governor Andronikos Asen captured Akova along with Karytaina and other castles of central Peloponnese, bringing the barony into what became the Despotate of the Morea.

british-occupation-of-saint-domingue.t: Britain's costly five-year attempt to seize revolutionary Saint-Domingue, which cost it tens of thousands of soldiers, mostly to yellow fever.
british-occupation-of-saint-domingue.o: Royalist French planters, alarmed by the abolition of slavery, invited Britain to take over Saint-Domingue after war broke out with revolutionary France. British troops from Jamaica landed at Jérémie and Môle Saint-Nicolas in September 1793 and captured Port-au-Prince in June 1794.
british-occupation-of-saint-domingue.r: The occupiers governed the coastal towns they held in alliance with planters and with restored slavery, relying heavily on locally raised black and coloured troops. They never controlled the interior. Yellow fever and malaria devastated the reinforcements sent from Britain, while Toussaint Louverture, now fighting for the French Republic, and André Rigaud pressed them from the north and south.
british-occupation-of-saint-domingue.e: With losses mounting, Brigadier Thomas Maitland negotiated an evacuation with Toussaint and withdrew the last British forces in 1798, also reaching a secret trade agreement. The failure helped Toussaint consolidate power and strengthened the path to Haitian independence.

bangkalan-kingdom.t: West Madurese realm of the Cakraningrat dynasty, first a vassal of Mataram and then a key Dutch ally on the island of Madura.
bangkalan-kingdom.o: After Sultan Agung of the Mataram Sultanate conquered Madura in 1624, he installed a local prince, Raden Praseno, as Cakraningrat I to rule the western half of the island from Sampang. The dynasty owed loyalty to Mataram, but its Madurese subjects were restless, and the prince Trunajaya led a great rebellion against Mataram from 1674 to 1680.
bangkalan-kingdom.r: The Cakraningrat princes ruled a dry island of salt pans, cattle and fishing whose men served as soldiers across Java. Cakraningrat IV turned against Mataram and the Dutch East India Company in the 1740s and was exiled to the Cape in 1745. His successors moved the court to Bangkalan and became firm Company allies.
bangkalan-kingdom.e: Bangkalan troops served the Dutch in Java and beyond, and in the early 19th century its rulers received the title of sultan. The Dutch gradually reduced their powers and abolished the kingdom in 1885, placing West Madura under direct colonial rule as part of the Dutch East Indies.

british-mauritius.t: The sugar island taken from France in 1810, transformed by Indian indentured labour into a mainly Indian-descended society.
british-mauritius.o: Britain seized the French Isle de France in December 1810, landing at Cap Malheureux months after a French naval victory at Grand Port, in order to stop French raiders preying on Indian Ocean shipping. The island was ceded in the 1814 Treaty of Paris, renamed Mauritius, and its first governor, Robert Farquhar, ruled from Port Louis.
british-mauritius.r: The capitulation let Franco-Mauritian planters keep their French law, language and Catholic church, and sugar became the island's economy. After slavery ended in 1835, nearly half a million indentured labourers arrived from India through the immigration depot now called Aapravasi Ghat, so that Hindus and Muslims of Indian origin became the majority while Creoles and French-speaking whites kept much economic power.
british-mauritius.e: After constitutional reforms and the rise of the Labour Party, Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968 under Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, and a republic in 1992. The Chagos Archipelago, detached by Britain in 1965, remained disputed.

buyeo.t: A kingdom of the Manchurian plains that Goguryeo and Baekje both claimed as their ancestral homeland, and a long-time ally of Han China.
buyeo.o: Buyeo appears in Chinese sources in the 2nd century BCE as a farming and herding kingdom on the Songhua river plain around modern Jilin. Its founding legend of Dongmyeong, born of sunlight and escaping across a river on a bridge of fish and turtles, was later borrowed for the founder of Goguryeo.
buyeo.r: The king shared power with four great officials named after animals: horse, ox, pig and dog, each governing a region. Kings could be blamed and deposed for bad harvests. Laws were strict, the yeonggo festival in the twelfth month honoured heaven, and nobles were buried with human victims. Buyeo usually sided with Chinese dynasties against Goguryeo and the Xianbei.
buyeo.e: Xianbei raids under the Murong in 285 and 346 devastated the kingdom, and King Uiryeo took his own life in the first. Weakened and pressed by the Mohe, the last king surrendered to Goguryeo in 494. Baekje's later name Nambuyeo recalled the link.

bit-yakin.t: The most powerful Chaldean tribe of southern Babylonia, home of Merodach-baladan, the long-time rival of the kings of Assyria.
bit-yakin.o: Bit-Yakin occupied the marshes and coastland at the head of the Gulf, the region once called the Sealand. Its fortified centre was Dur-Yakin. Like the other Chaldean tribes, it appears in Assyrian annals in the 9th century BCE, when its chiefs paid tribute to Shalmaneser III.
bit-yakin.r: Its sheikhs grew rich from date palms, Gulf trade and control of the marsh routes, which also made their land a refuge from Assyrian armies. Merodach-baladan II (Marduk-apla-iddina) made himself king of Babylon from 721 to 710 BCE and again in 703 BCE, allied with the Neo-Elamite kingdom and sent envoys as far as Judah, an embassy mentioned in the Bible.
bit-yakin.e: Sargon II took Dur-Yakin in 709 BCE, and Sennacherib pursued the tribe's refugees by ship to Elam in 694 BCE. Merodach-baladan's grandson Nabu-bel-shumati joined Shamash-shum-ukin's revolt and died in Elam around 648 BCE, after which Bit-Yakin disappears as a power.

baudh-state.t: A princely state on the upper Mahanadi in Odisha, whose capital Boudh holds Buddhist and Hindu remains, ruled by Rajas until 1948.
baudh-state.o: Tradition places the founding of the ruling dynasty around 1400. The town's name is linked to the Buddhist remains found there, including a large seated Buddha image.
baudh-state.r: Baudh was an inland state of farmland and forest on the Mahanadi. It was linked with the neighbouring Kondh hill tracts, which were separated from it under British rule in the 19th century. It paid tribute to the Marathas and later belonged to the Orissa Tributary States. Its internal history is poorly documented.
baudh-state.e: Baudh merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now Boudh district, Odisha.

bellovaci.t: The most powerful of the Belgic peoples, around Beauvais, who fought Caesar in 57 BCE and led one of the last Gallic revolts in 51 BCE.
bellovaci.o: The Bellovaci lived in the modern Oise and Picardy around Beauvais. Caesar was told that they could field a hundred thousand men and had promised sixty thousand to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
bellovaci.r: Their society was led by a warrior nobility, and they had ties to the Aedui. Large sanctuaries such as Gournay-sur-Aronde, with displays of weapons and sacrificed animals, show their religious practice.
bellovaci.e: In 57 BCE they surrendered at Bratuspantium after the Aeduan Diviciacus spoke for them. In 51 BCE they rose under Correus, who died fighting. Under Rome their chief town became Caesaromagus, later Beauvais.

bhaisaunda-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs near Kalinjar in Bundelkhand, granted to the Brahmin family that surrendered the fort to the British in 1812.
bhaisaunda-state.o: Bhaisaunda was one of the small holdings given in 1812 to members of the Chaube family, Brahmin governors of Kalinjar fort under the rulers of Panna, when they handed the fortress over to the British.
bhaisaunda-state.r: It was a minor estate of a few villages under the Bundelkhand Agency. Little else of its history is recorded.
bhaisaunda-state.e: After independence Bhaisaunda was merged into Vindhya Pradesh with the other Bundelkhand states and absorbed by 1950.

beirut.t: Beirut, a Late Bronze Age Canaanite port known from the Amarna letters, ancestor of the modern Lebanese capital.
beirut.o: Biruta grew on a promontory on the central Lebanese coast, settled since prehistory. By the 15th century BCE it was a small walled port town under the overlordship of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom.
beirut.r: Its ruler Ammunira wrote to the pharaoh in the Amarna letters, promising loyalty and sending reports. When Rib-Hadda of Byblos was driven out of his city by a rebellion, he took refuge in Beirut. Excavations in the city centre after the civil war uncovered its Bronze Age walls.
beirut.e: The Canaanite town shared the decline of the coast in the 12th century BCE, and in the Iron Age remained in the shadow of Sidon and Tyre. It later grew into the Roman colony of Berytus.

banu-khurasan.t: A local dynasty that ruled Tunis as an independent city-state after the Zirid collapse, until the Almohad conquest.
banu-khurasan.o: After the Banu Hilal defeated the Zirid emirate and Kairouan was abandoned in 1057, Tunis broke away. Around 1059 its notables chose Abd al-Haqq ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Khurasan, from a local family of notables, as ruler, founding the Khurasanid dynasty in the old port city.
banu-khurasan.r: The Khurasanids ruled Tunis and its hinterland as a small Sunni city-state, at first recognising the Hammadid emirate as overlord to secure protection from the Arab tribes and the Zirids of Mahdia. They paid the Bedouin for peace, strengthened the walls and encouraged trade by sea. Ahmad ibn Abd al-Aziz, the most notable ruler, built palaces and gathered scholars at his court.
banu-khurasan.e: The dynasty was briefly displaced by the Hammadids in 1128, but returned. In 1159 the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min took Tunis, ending its independence, and the city later became the capital of the Hafsids.

bit-hamban.t: A Zagros principality on the great road from Mesopotamia into Iran, repeatedly raided and finally annexed by Assyria.
bit-hamban.o: Bit-Hamban lay in the western Zagros, probably around the upper Diyala and the Kermanshah region, along the route later called the Great Khorasan Road. It appears in Assyrian annals from the reign of Shalmaneser III in the mid-9th century BCE as a land of local lords.
bit-hamban.r: Nothing is known of its institutions beyond Assyrian campaign reports, which list towns captured and tribute of horses and livestock. Its rulers seem to have been local chiefs rather than kings of a centralised state, sometimes in league with neighbours such as Parsua and Ellipi.
bit-hamban.e: Tiglath-Pileser III incorporated Bit-Hamban into the Assyrian Empire in 744 BCE, and under Sargon II it formed part of the Assyrian provincial system in the Zagros. It disappears from the record by about 700 BCE.

berar-sultanate.t: The smallest of the Deccan sultanates, ruled by the Imad Shahi dynasty from Ellichpur in the Berar plain of central India.
berar-sultanate.o: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, a Bahmani governor of Berar who was originally a Hindu convert from Vijayanagara territory, declared independence around 1490 as the Bahmani Sultanate broke up. He ruled from Ellichpur and the fort of Gawilgarh, founding the Imad Shahi dynasty.
berar-sultanate.r: Berar was a fertile cotton and grain-growing region, but the sultanate was weak and survived by balancing between its neighbours, the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, the Khandesh Sultanate and the Bijapur Sultanate. Its rulers strengthened the hill fortresses of Gawilgarh and Narnala. Few literary sources describe its internal history.
berar-sultanate.e: Murtaza Nizam Shah of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate invaded Berar and annexed it in 1574, ending the Imad Shahi line. Berar later passed to the Mughal Empire, then to the Nizams of Hyderabad and finally the British.

bhadva-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, one of its many small hereditary estates.
bhadva-state.o: Bhadva was a small estate in Kathiawar held by a local Rajput family from around 1700. Its founding is not well documented.
bhadva-state.r: The ruler held a few villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Few further details are recorded in standard works.
bhadva-state.e: Bhadva merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960, in Rajkot district.

batavi.t: Germanic people of the Rhine delta who served as Rome's elite soldiers and imperial bodyguards, then rose in a great revolt in 69 CE.
batavi.o: Tacitus says the Batavi were a branch of the Chatti who, after a quarrel at home, settled on the island between the Rhine and the Waal, the modern Betuwe in the Netherlands, probably in the later 1st century BCE.
batavi.r: Instead of paying tribute, they supplied Rome with soldiers: cavalry famous for swimming rivers in full armour, auxiliary cohorts and the emperors' German bodyguard. Their noble families commanded these units, and their chief town Batavodurum stood at Nijmegen.
batavi.e: In 69 CE Julius Civilis led a revolt joined by the Cananefates, Frisii and Treveri, which was crushed in 70 CE. The Batavi resumed service, and Ulpia Noviomagus (Nijmegen) became a Roman town. They faded in the Frankish period, but the Dutch long saw them as ancestors.

bijawar-state.t: A Bundela Rajput state of Bundelkhand, founded in the 1760s by a descendant of Chhatrasal.
bijawar-state.o: Bijawar was founded around 1765 by Bir Singh Deo, a Bundela of the family of Chhatrasal, who carved out his own territory as Bundela power fragmented.
bijawar-state.r: The British confirmed the state by sanad in the early 19th century. Bijawar was an 11-gun salute state of the Bundelkhand Agency, ruled by a Maharaja over a hilly, partly forested territory. Little else of its internal history is recorded.
bijawar-state.e: After independence Bijawar was merged into Vindhya Pradesh and absorbed by 1950; it is now in Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh.

black-sea-cossack-host.t: A Cossack army formed from former Zaporozhians, which settled the Kuban frontier and founded the city now called Krasnodar.
black-sea-cossack-host.o: In 1787, on the eve of war with the Ottoman Empire, Prince Grigory Potemkin gathered former Zaporozhian Cossacks into the Host of Loyal Zaporozhians. Led by Sydir Bilyi, Zakhary Chepiha and Anton Holovaty, they fought at Ochakiv and Izmail, and in 1790 they were renamed the Black Sea Cossack Host.
black-sea-cossack-host.r: In 1792 Catherine II granted the Host the lands of the Taman peninsula and the right bank of the Kuban, and in 1793 they founded Yekaterinodar as their capital. The Cossacks kept elected officers and a Zaporozhian tradition, farming and guarding a fortified line against the Circassians across the Kuban.
black-sea-cossack-host.e: The Host fought throughout the Caucasian War. In 1860 it was merged with part of the Caucasus Line Cossack Host to form the Kuban Cossack Host. Its Ukrainian heritage shaped the speech and culture of the Kuban region.

bondelswarts.t: A Nama community of southern Namibia centred on Warmbad, known for its uprisings against German and later South African rule.
bondelswarts.o: The Bondelswarts, in Nama !Gami-ǂnun, were a Khoekhoe-speaking Nama group living north of the Orange River. In 1805 the London Missionary Society founded a mission at Warmbad among them, and Wesleyans took it over in the 1830s; Warmbad became the seat of their kapteins.
bondelswarts.r: Like other Nama communities they were governed by a hereditary kaptein, here of the Christian family, with a council of elders. They lived by herding cattle, sheep and goats in the dry south, traded with the Cape and many adopted Christianity and Cape Dutch through the mission.
bondelswarts.e: In 1903 the killing of their kaptein Jan Abraham Christian by German officials sparked a rising, which merged into the wider Nama war; they made peace at Ukamas in December 1906 and lost most of their land. Their 1922 rebellion against a South African dog tax was crushed with aircraft.

byzacena.t: The late Roman province of central Tunisia, an olive-growing land of prosperous towns governed from Hadrumetum.
byzacena.o: Around 303 Diocletian divided Africa Proconsularis into smaller provinces as part of his reorganisation of the empire. The southern part of the old province, the region known as Byzacium, became Byzacena, with its capital at Hadrumetum (Sousse), and was governed by a consularis within the Diocese of Africa.
byzacena.r: Byzacena was one of the richest farming regions of the Mediterranean, covered with olive groves whose oil was shipped to Rome and beyond. Towns such as Thysdrus, with its great amphitheatre at El Djem, Sufetula and Thaenae flourished. The province had many bishoprics and was strongly affected by the Donatist controversy. Large imperial and private estates employed tenant farmers, the coloni.
byzacena.e: The Vandals took control after capturing Carthage in 439, and the region was part of the Vandal Kingdom until Justinian's reconquest in 534 restored a province of Byzacena under the Praetorian Prefecture of Africa. Berber kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Capsus held its southern edges.

bailiwick-of-guernsey.t: A self-governing British Crown Dependency of Channel Islands, held by the crown as heir of the Dukes of Normandy since 1204.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.o: Guernsey belonged to the Duchy of Normandy from the 10th century. When King John lost continental Normandy to Philip II of France in 1204, the islands stayed with the English crown, and a separate bailiwick, under its own bailiff and royal court, developed for Guernsey, Alderney, Sark and the smaller islands.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.r: Guernsey kept Norman customary law, its Royal Court of jurats and, later, the States of Deliberation as its parliament. Its economy rested on fishing, knitting, privateering and later tomatoes, horticulture and finance. Saint Peter Port was a major harbour. During the English Civil War it sided with Parliament, and Victor Hugo lived there in exile from 1855.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.e: Guernsey was occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom, with its own government, laws and taxes, while the UK handles defence and international relations.

bamra-state.t: A princely state of the Sambalpur hills in western Odisha whose 19th-century Raja made its capital Deogarh a centre of Odia printing and literature.
bamra-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from the Eastern Ganga dynasty, and tradition dates the state to the mid-16th century. It was one of the chiefships in the orbit of Sambalpur State.
bamra-state.r: Bamra, also called Bamanda, was a hilly, forested state. It came under the Bhonsles of the Nagpur Kingdom and later British supervision. Raja Basudeb Sudhal Deb (r. 1869–1903) set up a printing press at Deogarh that published an Odia newspaper and books, and introduced schools and public works.
bamra-state.e: Bamra merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948, and Deogarh is now the headquarters of Deogarh district.
