baluchistan-states-union.t: A short-lived federation of the four princely states of Balochistan within Pakistan, led by the Khan of Kalat.
baluchistan-states-union.o: In 1952 Kalat, Kharan, Makran State and Las Bela State, which had acceded to Pakistan in 1948, were combined into the Baluchistan States Union. The Khan of Kalat, Ahmad Yar Khan, became its head as Khan-e-Azam.
baluchistan-states-union.r: The union had a council of the rulers and a small administration based at Kalat, with Pakistan's government retaining control of defence, foreign affairs and communications. It covered a vast, thinly populated territory of pastoralists, farmers and coastal fishermen.
baluchistan-states-union.e: In 1955 the union was dissolved and merged into West Pakistan under the One Unit scheme, ending the political role of the Baloch rulers. Its lands are now part of Balochistan province.

balearic-islanders.t: The tower-building peoples of Mallorca and Menorca, whose stone talaiots and taulas still dot the islands and whose slingers fought for Carthage and Rome.
balearic-islanders.o: From around 1000 BCE the islanders of Mallorca and Menorca developed what archaeologists call the Talaiotic culture, named after the talaiots, massive dry-stone towers that dominated fortified villages. It grew out of the earlier Naviform culture of boat-shaped houses and stone tombs such as the Naveta des Tudons on Menorca.
balearic-islanders.r: There was no single state: the islands were divided among village communities, probably led by local chiefs, living from herding, farming and some trade with Phoenician and Punic merchants, especially from nearby Ebusus. Menorca's T-shaped taulas stood in sanctuary enclosures. The islanders were famed throughout the Mediterranean as slingers and served as mercenaries in Carthaginian armies, including Hannibal's.
balearic-islanders.e: Accused of sheltering pirates, the islands were conquered in 123 BCE by the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus, who took the name Balearicus and founded the towns of Palma and Pollentia. Talaiotic traditions faded under Roman rule, but hundreds of monuments survive.

burgraviate-of-nuremberg.t: The castle office at Nuremberg that gave the Hohenzollerns their first foothold in Franconia, the start of their rise to kings of Prussia.
burgraviate-of-nuremberg.o: Around 1105 the Salian emperors appointed burgraves to command the royal castle of Nuremberg. The first family, the Raabs, died out around 1190, and Frederick of Zollern, a Swabian noble married to the Raabs' heiress, became burgrave in 1192, founding the Franconian Hohenzollern line.
burgraviate-of-nuremberg.r: The burgraves held the castle, rights of justice and lands around Nuremberg, and gradually built a territory in Franconia, acquiring Ansbach in 1331 and Kulmbach and Bayreuth. Frederick III of Nuremberg helped elect Rudolf I in 1273. The city of Nuremberg itself grew into a free imperial city and rival.
burgraviate-of-nuremberg.e: In 1415 Burgrave Frederick VI received the Margraviate of Brandenburg as Elector Frederick I. In 1427 he sold the burgrave's castle to the city of Nuremberg. His Franconian lands became the margraviates of Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Kulmbach (Bayreuth).

bessi.t: Thracian highland people of the Rhodopes and Haemus, keepers of a famous oracle of Dionysus and stubborn rebels against Rome.
bessi.o: Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BCE, names the Bessi as the priests of the oracle of Dionysus in the mountains of the Satrae. By later centuries they were a distinct people of the upper Hebrus (Maritsa) and Rhodope ranges in modern Bulgaria.
bessi.r: A loose tribal people of mountain country, the Bessi combined herding, mining and raiding. Their religious standing as guardians of the Dionysian sanctuary gave them prestige among Thracians. They clashed with the Odrysian Kingdom and with Macedon, and later raided Roman Macedonia.
bessi.e: Marcus Licinius Crassus subdued them in 29 BCE, but in 11 BCE the priest Vologases led a major revolt that took years to crush. Their name survived under Rome, and a Bessian language was reportedly still used in monastic worship in the 6th century CE.

baria-state.t: A Chauhan Rajput state in eastern Gujarat founded by descendants of the last Rajput rulers of Champaner after its fall to the Gujarat Sultanate.
baria-state.o: When Mahmud Begada of the Gujarat Sultanate took Champaner and Pavagadh in 1484, the defeated Chauhan Rajput rulers' descendants withdrew into the hills to the east. By tradition they founded Devgadh Baria in 1524, and it became the capital of their state.
baria-state.r: Baria was a forested, hilly state with a large Bhil population. It paid tribute to the Marathas and later came under British supervision in the Rewa Kantha Agency. Its later rulers built a palace and introduced modern administration in the early 20th century.
baria-state.e: Baria merged into Bombay State in 1948. Its last ruler, Jaideepsinhji, later served as a minister in Gujarat. Devgadh Baria is now in Dahod district.

bakwena-chiefdom.t: The Tswana chiefdom of the Kwena, whose ruler Sechele I was David Livingstone's only convert and a shrewd defender of his people.
bakwena-chiefdom.o: The Bakwena trace their origin to a split from the Bahurutshe and later gave rise to the Bangwato and Bangwaketse through further divisions. By the 18th century the Kwena were settled in what is now south-eastern Botswana, though they were scattered during the wars of the 1820s.
bakwena-chiefdom.r: Sechele I rebuilt the chiefdom from the 1830s, ruling through the kgotla and ward system. He welcomed David Livingstone, was baptised in 1848, and kept trade routes open to the north. In 1852 Transvaal Boers attacked his town at Dimawe, but Sechele survived and made the Kwena a regional power, settling at Molepolole in the 1860s.
bakwena-chiefdom.e: Fearing Boer expansion, the Tswana chiefs accepted British protection, and in 1885 Kweneng became part of the Bechuanaland Protectorate. The chiefdom continued under colonial rule and is part of independent Botswana.

banu-ghaniya-majorca.t: The last Almoravid state, ruled from Majorca by the Banu Ghaniya, who waged a long war against the Almohads from the Balearics to Ifriqiya.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.o: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Ghaniya, of an Almoravid family related to the ruling dynasty, governed the Balearic Islands from about 1126. When the Almoravid Empire collapsed in the 1140s, he kept the islands as an independent emirate loyal to the Abbasid caliph.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.r: Under Ishaq ibn Muhammad (c. 1155-1183) Majorca prospered on trade and corsair raids, and made treaties with Genoa and Pisa. In 1184 Ali ibn Ghaniya invaded North Africa, seizing Bejaia and starting a war against the Almohads in Ifriqiya that lasted half a century.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.e: The Almohads conquered Majorca in 1203, killing its ruler Abd Allah ibn Ishaq, though the family fought on in Ifriqiya. James I of Aragon took Majorca in 1229, later forming the Kingdom of Majorca.

bukharan-peoples-soviet-republic.t: The Soviet-backed republic established after the Red Army stormed Bukhara in 1920, led by the Young Bukharan reformer Fayzulla Khodzhayev.
bukharan-peoples-soviet-republic.o: In September 1920 the Red Army under Mikhail Frunze, supporting a revolt by the Young Bukharans and Bukharan communists, captured Bukhara and drove out the last emir. The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed in October 1920.
bukharan-peoples-soviet-republic.r: Led by Fayzulla Khodzhayev as chairman of the council of people's nazirs, the republic carried out land and educational reforms but remained dependent on Soviet troops and money. It faced the Basmachi resistance, which in 1921 and 1922 was joined by the Ottoman general Enver Pasha, killed in eastern Bukhara in 1922. It became the Bukharan Soviet Socialist Republic in 1924.
bukharan-peoples-soviet-republic.e: In the national delimitation of 1924 its territory was divided between the Uzbek SSR, the Tajik ASSR and the Turkmen SSR. Khodzhayev became head of the Uzbek government and was executed in 1938.

bastar-state.t: A vast forest kingdom in central India founded by refugees from the Kakatiya court, famous for its goddess Danteshwari and its 75-day Dussehra festival.
bastar-state.o: By tradition, Annama Deva, a brother of the last Kakatiya king Prataparudra, fled north after the Delhi Sultanate took Warangal in 1323 and established a kingdom among the Gond and other peoples of the Bastar plateau. The family goddess Danteshwari, enshrined at Dantewada, became the patron deity of the state.
bastar-state.r: Bastar was thinly populated, densely forested and overwhelmingly Adivasi, with Gond, Maria, Muria and Halba communities. The Rajas ruled through local headmen and ritual ties, celebrated in the long Bastar Dussehra. In the 18th century the state became tributary to the Bhonsles of the Nagpur Kingdom, passing under British control in 1853. The Bhumkal rebellion of 1910 against forest restrictions was suppressed by British troops.
bastar-state.e: Bastar merged into the Central Provinces, later Madhya Pradesh, in 1948. Its former ruler Pravir Chandra Bhanj Deo was killed by police at his palace in 1966. Bastar is now a region of Chhattisgarh.

busoga-principalities.t: A cluster of small Basoga principalities east of the Nile, united under the British as a kingdom with an elected ruler, the Kyabazinga.
busoga-principalities.o: From about the 16th century the land between the Nile, Lake Victoria and Lake Kyoga was divided among numerous small principalities, many of whose ruling families traced their origins to Bunyoro and its legendary hunter Mukama. No central kingdom emerged, and the principalities often paid tribute to the more powerful Kingdom of Buganda.
busoga-principalities.r: Each principality was ruled by a hereditary chief with clan heads and village leaders. The economy rested on plantains, cattle and fishing on the lakes. Under the Uganda Protectorate the British created a council of chiefs and, from 1906, the office of Kyabazinga, chosen among the senior chiefs, to rule Busoga as a single unit from Bugembe near Jinja.
busoga-principalities.e: The Kyabazinga's office was abolished with the other Ugandan monarchies in 1967 and restored as a cultural institution in 1995. Kyabazinga William Wilberforce Nadiope served as Uganda's vice-president in the 1960s.
busoga-principalities.re: Traditional religion, later Christianity and Islam

baoni-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state in Bundelkhand founded for the former Mughal vizier Imad-ul-Mulk, named after its 52 villages.
baoni-state.o: Ghazi-ud-din Khan Imad-ul-Mulk, the Mughal vizier who had deposed Ahmad Shah Bahadur and murdered Alamgir II, later took refuge with the Marathas. Around 1784 the Peshwa granted him 52 villages (baoni) in Bundelkhand, which became the state of Baoni with its seat at Kadaura.
baoni-state.r: Baoni was an 11-gun salute state of the Bundelkhand Agency ruled by a Nawab over a mostly Hindu farming population. Little else of its internal history is recorded.
baoni-state.e: After independence Baoni joined Vindhya Pradesh in 1948, and its lands were later transferred to Jalaun district of Uttar Pradesh.

banten-sultanate.t: The pepper sultanate of western Java, a leading Asian port of the 17th century until the Dutch East India Company reduced it to a vassal.
banten-sultanate.o: Around 1527 forces from Demak and Cirebon, led by Sunan Gunung Jati and his son Maulana Hasanuddin, took the port of Banten from the Sunda Kingdom. Hasanuddin became its first ruler. In 1579 his son Maulana Yusuf captured Pakuan Pajajaran, ending the Sunda Kingdom.
banten-sultanate.r: Banten became one of Southeast Asia's great pepper markets, drawing Chinese, Indian, English and Danish merchants; the first Dutch fleet arrived in 1596, and the English opened a factory in 1602. Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, from 1651, built canals and a navy and challenged Dutch Batavia. The Surosowan palace and Great Mosque date from this era.
banten-sultanate.e: In 1682 Ageng's son, Sultan Haji, sought Dutch help against his father, and the Company won control of Banten's trade. Herman Willem Daendels destroyed the palace in 1808, and Thomas Stamford Raffles abolished the sultanate in 1813.

byzantium.t: Megarian colony on the Bosporus that controlled the passage to the Black Sea and later became Constantinople.
byzantium.o: Settlers from Megara, led according to tradition by Byzas, founded Byzantium c. 667 BCE on the European promontory between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara. The site commanded the Bosporus, the only sea route between the Aegean and the Black Sea.
byzantium.r: Byzantium grew rich from tuna fishing and tolls on shipping, especially the grain trade. It came under the Achaemenid Empire, was taken by the Spartan regent Pausanias in 478 BCE and then joined the Delian League, revolting in 440 BCE. Its resistance to Philip II's siege of 340 to 339 BCE was celebrated. In 220 BCE Rhodes went to war over its new tolls.
byzantium.e: Byzantium allied with Rome in the 2nd century BCE and kept its freedom until Vespasian brought it into a Roman province c. 73 CE. Constantine refounded it as Constantinople in 330 CE, capital of the Byzantine Empire.

banat-of-craiova.t: Habsburg-ruled Oltenia, the western third of Wallachia, held by Austria for two decades after the Treaty of Passarowitz.
banat-of-craiova.o: In the Austro-Turkish war of 1716 to 1718 Habsburg forces occupied Oltenia, the part of Wallachia west of the Olt river. The Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 ceded it to the Habsburg monarchy, which organised it as a province with its seat at Craiova, the traditional residence of the Wallachian bans.
banat-of-craiova.r: The province was governed by an imperial administration with a local boyar, Gheorghe Cantacuzino, as ban at first. Vienna introduced a census, regular taxes, a postal service and stricter control over boyars and monasteries, reforms that curbed noble privileges but raised burdens; many peasants fled across the Olt. Orthodox religion and Romanian-speaking society remained unchanged.
banat-of-craiova.e: Habsburg defeat in the war of 1737 to 1739 led to the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, which returned Oltenia to Wallachia under Ottoman suzerainty. The episode left detailed Austrian maps and surveys of the region.

baghat-state.t: A small Rajput hill state of the Shimla hills whose capital at Solan grew into one of the main towns of Himachal Pradesh.
baghat-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins. Its name is often explained as 'many passes'.
baghat-state.r: Baghat was a small hill state on the road from Kalka to Shimla. It was occupied by Gurkhas in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. With the coming of the Kalka-Shimla road and railway, Solan became its capital and grew as a market town.
baghat-state.e: Baghat merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948, and Solan is now the headquarters of Solan district.

bozhou-chiefdom.t: The hereditary domain of the Yang family in northern Guizhou, which ruled for seven centuries as a native chieftaincy under Chinese dynasties until its destruction in 1600.
bozhou-chiefdom.o: According to family tradition, Yang Duan, a man from Taiyuan, recovered Bozhou, around modern Zunyi, from Nanzhao forces in 876 and was granted hereditary authority over it. His descendants ruled the mountainous region as local lords, accepting nominal titles from successive Chinese courts.
bozhou-chiefdom.r: The Yang lords governed a mixed population of Han settlers and Miao, Gelao and other peoples as tusi, native chieftains who paid tribute and supplied troops while running their own affairs. The Song, Yuan and Ming dynasties confirmed their titles. During the Mongol wars the Southern Song built the mountain fortress of Hailongtun in 1257, later the seat of the Yang family.
bozhou-chiefdom.e: Yang Yinglong rebelled against the Ming Empire in 1589. In 1600 a large Ming army under Li Hualong stormed Hailongtun and Yang Yinglong killed himself. The chieftaincy was abolished and replaced by regular prefectures under direct imperial rule.

bedulu-kingdom.t: The Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Bali under the Warmadewa line, ruling from Bedulu and Pejeng until Majapahit's conquest in 1343.
bedulu-kingdom.o: The Belanjong pillar of 914 at Sanur records Sri Kesari Warmadewa, the first known Balinese king, campaigning on the island. His Warmadewa dynasty ruled from the Pejeng and Bedulu area, the fertile heart of Bali near modern Ubud, for over three centuries.
bedulu-kingdom.r: Royal charters in Old Balinese, later Old Javanese, show irrigation communities, ancestors of the subak system, and temples endowed with land. King Udayana married the Javanese princess Mahendradatta, and their son Airlangga later ruled Kahuripan in Java. The rock-cut sanctuaries of Goa Gajah and Gunung Kawi, the latter linked to King Anak Wungsu, date from this period.
bedulu-kingdom.e: In 1343 Majapahit troops under Gajah Mada and Adityawarman defeated the last king, remembered as Sri Astasura Ratna Bumi Banten. Majapahit installed a Javanese dynasty that ruled from Samprangan and then the Kingdom of Gelgel, shaping later Balinese court culture.

bishopric-of-culm.t: One of the four Prussian dioceses set up in 1243, ruling the land of Löbau and passing under the Polish crown in 1466.
bishopric-of-culm.o: In 1243 the papal legate William of Modena divided conquered Prussia into four dioceses: Culm, Pomesania, Warmia and Samland. Culm covered the Chełmno land, which Konrad of Masovia had granted to the Teutonic Order, and the bishop received a third of the diocese as his own territory, chiefly around Löbau.
bishopric-of-culm.r: The bishops' cathedral stood at Culmsee (Chełmża), while they resided at the castle of Löbau. The cathedral chapter was incorporated into the Teutonic Order in the 13th century, tying the bishopric closely to the Order's state. Chełmno law, granted in the Culm charter of 1233, became the model for town and land rights across Prussia.
bishopric-of-culm.e: During the Thirteen Years' War, the Prussian estates rebelled against the Order, and the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 placed the Chełmno land under the Polish crown as part of Royal Prussia. The bishops became Polish senators, and the diocese continued as a church province.

bructeri.t: A Germanic people of Westphalia who fought Rome alongside Arminius and sheltered the seeress Veleda during the Batavian revolt.
bructeri.o: The Bructeri lived between the upper Ems and the Lippe, in what is now Westphalia. They appear in Roman sources from 12 BCE, when Drusus fought them on the Ems. In 9 CE they joined Arminius against Varus and captured the eagle of the Nineteenth Legion, which Germanicus' general Stertinius recovered in 15.
bructeri.r: Their leadership was in the hands of chiefs and an influential religious figure: the seeress Veleda, who lived in a tower near the Lippe, foretold the success of the Batavian revolt of 69 and was consulted by other peoples. Around 98, Tacitus reports that neighbouring tribes had nearly wiped out the Bructeri while Romans watched.
bructeri.e: The Bructeri survived that defeat and are mentioned again in the 4th century as part of the Franks. Their district, the Boructuari, was among the peoples evangelised by Saint Suitbert around 700, before the Saxons overran it.

brunei-sultanate.t: A Malay sultanate of northern Borneo which in the 16th century ruled coasts from Sarawak to Manila and survives as the independent state of Brunei.
brunei-sultanate.o: Chinese records mention a kingdom called Po-ni in northwest Borneo from the 10th century. Brunei tradition holds that its ruler Awang Alak Betatar accepted Islam and became Sultan Muhammad Shah, the register dating this to 1368. The early capital was Kota Batu on the Brunei River.
brunei-sultanate.r: Under Sultan Bolkiah around 1500 Brunei reached its height, controlling much of Borneo's coast and allied ports in the Philippines, including Maynila. Its wealth came from trade in camphor, pepper and Chinese goods, and its water village impressed Antonio Pigafetta in 1521. Spain attacked in the Castilian War of 1578.
brunei-sultanate.e: In the 19th century Brunei lost Sarawak to James Brooke and Sabah to the British North Borneo Company. It became a British protectorate in 1888, oil was found at Seria in 1929, and it declined to join Malaysia in 1963. Brunei became fully independent in 1984 under Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah.

bigerriones.t: Aquitanian people of the high Pyrenean valleys around Tarbes, who gave their name to Bigorre.
bigerriones.o: The Bigerriones lived in the upper Adour valley and the Pyrenean foothills of the modern Hautes-Pyrénées. Caesar lists them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
bigerriones.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Like other Aquitani they spoke a language related to Basque, and their economy combined mountain herding with farming in the valleys.
bigerriones.e: Under Rome their chief town was Turba, later Tarbes, within the province of Aquitania and then Novempopulana. Their name passed to the medieval County of Bigorre.

banganapalle-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state in the Rayalaseema country of Andhra, best known for the mango variety that bears its name.
banganapalle-state.o: Banganapalle was granted in the 1660s by the Bijapur sultanate, then under Mughal pressure, to a Muslim officer whose descendants became its Nawabs. After a period of disputed succession the line of the Nawabs was confirmed under British protection.
banganapalle-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a small enclave surrounded by the Madras Presidency, with a mostly Telugu-speaking Hindu population. It was one of the few princely states attached to the Madras government. The region's orchards produced the Banganapalle mango, now one of India's best-known varieties.
banganapalle-state.e: The last Nawab acceded to India, and Banganapalle merged into Madras Province in 1948. It became part of Andhra State in 1953 and now lies in Andhra Pradesh.

buayan-sultanate.t: An upriver Maguindanao sultanate on the Pulangi River of Mindanao, long the rival of the coastal Maguindanao Sultanate.
buayan-sultanate.o: Buayan was the upstream, sa raya, state of the Pulangi river basin in central Mindanao, while Maguindanao held the coast, sa ilud. Both traced their Islam to Sharif Kabungsuan, a Johor-born preacher of the early 16th century. Buayan's rulers controlled the rice-growing interior and its links with highland peoples.
buayan-sultanate.r: Buayan's datus governed through kinship networks and controlled trade in rice, slaves and forest goods passing down the river. In the 19th century, as Maguindanao weakened under Spanish pressure, Datu Uto of Buayan became the strongest leader in the Pulangi valley and acquired firearms through traders.
buayan-sultanate.e: Spanish expeditions in the 1880s forced Datu Uto to submit, though he kept much of his power. After 1899 the Americans took over Mindanao, and by 1905 Buayan's independence was ended. The area is now part of the Bangsamoro region.

british-somaliland.t: A British protectorate on the Gulf of Aden coast of Somalia, which fought a 20-year war with the Dervishes and became independent as Somaliland in 1960.
british-somaliland.o: Britain's interest in the northern Somali coast came from Aden, which depended on Somali livestock. Between 1884 and 1886 British officers signed treaties with the Isaaq, Gadabuursi, Warsangali and other clans, and after Egypt withdrew from Zeila and Berbera the protectorate was established, run at first from British India.
british-somaliland.r: British rule was thin and cheap, aimed at keeping the coast secure and the meat trade flowing. From 1899 the Dervish State of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan fought a long war against the British, ended in 1920 by a campaign that used aircraft. Pastoral clans kept their customary institutions under appointed elders and Islamic courts. Italy occupied the territory briefly in 1940 to 1941.
british-somaliland.e: On 26 June 1960 British Somaliland became independent as the State of Somaliland, which five days later united with the former Trust Territory of Somaliland to form the Somali Republic. Its borders were revived by the Republic of Somaliland in 1991.

baku-commune.t: A Bolshevik-led government that ruled Baku for a few months in 1918 and whose leaders became Soviet martyrs as the 26 Baku Commissars.
baku-commune.o: In March 1918 the Baku Soviet, dominated by Bolsheviks and supported by Armenian Dashnak forces, defeated Azerbaijani Musavat units in fighting known as the March Days, in which thousands of Muslims were killed. In April it formed the Baku Council of People's Commissars under Stepan Shaumian, part of the Russian SFSR.
baku-commune.r: The Commune nationalised the oil industry and the Caspian fleet and tried to supply Soviet Russia with oil. Its forces were mostly Armenian, and it was opposed by the Azerbaijani population. It faced an advance on Baku by the Ottoman-led Army of Islam, which defeated its troops in June and July 1918.
baku-commune.e: On 31 July 1918 the Commune resigned after the Baku Soviet voted to invite British help, and the Centrocaspian Dictatorship took over. Its leaders fled, were captured and shot near Krasnovodsk in September 1918, becoming the 26 Baku Commissars of Soviet legend.

cr.a: Неизвестный художник (не указан в выходных данных плаката; отсутствует авторская монограмма или подпись)

begteginid-dynasty.t: A Turkmen dynasty of atabegs at Erbil whose ruler Gökböri, Saladin's brother-in-law, made the city famous for celebrating the Prophet's birthday.
begteginid-dynasty.o: Zayn al-Din Ali Kuchuk, son of Begtegin, was a Turkmen officer of Imad al-Din Zengi who became governor of Erbil and other towns around 1144. Under the Zengid dynasty of Mosul he built up a personal domain in the plains east of the Tigris, which his descendants inherited.
begteginid-dynasty.r: His son Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri married Rabi'a Khatun, sister of Saladin, fought at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and received Erbil as an Ayyubid ally in 1190. He ruled until 1233, building hospitals, hostels for travellers, schools and orphanages, and staging lavish public celebrations of the Mawlid, the Prophet's birthday, among the earliest recorded. The biographer Ibn Khallikan, a native of Erbil, praised his generosity.
begteginid-dynasty.e: Gökböri died without a male heir in 1233 and bequeathed Erbil to the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir, who annexed it. The Mongols took the city in 1258.

basoda-state.t: A small Pathan Nawabi state in Malwa, a branch of the family that ruled Kurwai.
basoda-state.o: Basoda was founded around 1753 by a member of the Afghan family of Kurwai, one of several Pathan chiefships established in the area during the decline of Mughal power.
basoda-state.r: The Nawab ruled a small farming territory around the town of Basoda in the Bhopal Agency. Few details of its internal history are recorded.
basoda-state.e: After accession to India Basoda was merged into Madhya Bharat in 1948 and joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956; its lands are in Vidisha district.

bolognese-republic.t: The brief republic set up in Bologna in 1796 after the French expelled papal rule, which soon merged into the Cispadane Republic.
bolognese-republic.o: In June 1796 French troops entered Bologna, part of the Papal States, and the papal legate left. The city's Senate, under French protection, took over the government, and Bologna declared itself a free republic.
bolognese-republic.r: Bologna's old ruling families kept much of their influence, governing through the Senate and new committees while meeting French demands for money and art. The republic drafted a constitution in late 1796. It sent delegates to the congresses that united Bologna with Ferrara, Modena and Reggio.
bolognese-republic.e: By the end of 1796 Bologna had joined the Cispadane Republic, which in 1797 became part of the Cisalpine Republic.

bar-kokhba-state.t: The short-lived Jewish state of Simon bar Kosiba, whose revolt against Hadrian was the last great Jewish rising against Rome.
bar-kokhba-state.o: The revolt broke out in 132, probably provoked by Hadrian's plan to refound Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, and possibly by a ban on circumcision. Its leader, Simon bar Kosiba, was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', a messianic title reportedly endorsed by Rabbi Akiva.
bar-kokhba-state.r: Simon styled himself Nasi (prince) of Israel and dated documents by the 'redemption of Israel'. Coins overstruck on Roman issues showed the Temple facade and the slogan 'for the freedom of Jerusalem'. Letters and contracts found in caves of the Judaean Desert, notably Nahal Hever, show a working administration that leased state land, collected produce and gave terse orders to commanders, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek.
bar-kokhba-state.e: Hadrian brought in Julius Severus from Britain, who wore the rebels down with a war of sieges. The fortress of Betar fell in 135 or 136. Judea was devastated, renamed Syria Palaestina, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem.

bit-dakkuri.t: A Chaldean tribe settled south of Babylon around Borsippa, often in conflict with the old cities over land.
bit-dakkuri.o: Bit-Dakkuri, 'House of Dakkuru', was one of the leading Chaldean tribes of Babylonia, settled along the Euphrates between Babylon and Borsippa. It first appears in 850 BCE, when its chief Adinu paid tribute of gold, silver and ivory to Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire.
bit-dakkuri.r: Like other Chaldean groups, Bit-Dakkuri was ruled by sheikhs from walled towns, living from date groves, herding and trade. Its proximity to Babylon and Borsippa led to disputes with city dwellers over farmland. Its sheikhs swung between Assyrian loyalty and support for Babylonian rebels.
bit-dakkuri.e: Esarhaddon of Assyria removed its chief Shamash-ibni around 678 BCE and returned seized lands to the citizens of Babylon and Borsippa. The tribe fades from the sources by the mid-7th century BCE.

beylik-of-mani.t: Semi-autonomous Ottoman principality of the Mani peninsula, whose last bey, Petrobey Mavromichalis, helped launch the Greek War of Independence.
beylik-of-mani.o: The Maniots of the southern Peloponnese had always resisted Ottoman control. After the failed Orlov revolt of 1770 and the Russo-Turkish peace of 1774, the Ottomans gave up direct rule and in 1776 created a Beylik of Mani under the authority of the Kapudan Pasha, the Ottoman admiral, with a Maniot bey.
beylik-of-mani.r: The bey, chosen from the Maniot clans, paid a modest tribute and kept order, but power remained with the feuding chieftain families in their stone tower houses. Notable beys included Tzanetos Grigorakis and, from 1815, Petros Mavromichalis. The Mani was poor, with olive oil, piracy and a strong warrior tradition shaping its society.
beylik-of-mani.e: In March 1821 Petrobey Mavromichalis declared revolt at Areopolis and Kalamata, joining the Greek War of Independence. The beylik ended, and the Mani became part of the First Hellenic Republic, though its clans long resisted central government.

banka-pahari-state.t: A very small chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency, known almost only from British lists of the minor states of central India.
banka-pahari-state.o: Banka-Pahari was confirmed as a separate holding by the British in the early 19th century, as one of several small estates left from the break-up of Bundela power.
banka-pahari-state.r: It comprised only a handful of villages under a hereditary chief. Nothing else of note is recorded in standard sources.
banka-pahari-state.e: After independence Banka-Pahari was merged into Vindhya Pradesh with the other Bundelkhand states and absorbed by 1950.

barca.t: A Greek city of Cyrenaica founded by rebel Battiad princes, remembered for its brutal destruction by the Persians.
barca.o: Herodotus relates that around 560 BCE the brothers of King Arcesilaus II of the Kingdom of Cyrene quarrelled with him and founded Barca, on the plain inland from the coast (near modern al-Marj), with the support of local Libyans. The city soon became a rival of its mother city.
barca.r: Barca was a Greek city of mixed Greek and Libyan population, ruled at first by kings; Herodotus names a king Alazeir, whose daughter married Arcesilaus III of Cyrene. It was known for horse breeding and chariots. When Arcesilaus III was murdered there, his mother Pheretime called in the Persian governor of Egypt, Aryandes, whose army took Barca around 515 BCE by trickery after a long siege.
barca.e: Many Barcaeans were deported to Bactria. The city recovered as a member of the Cyrenaican cities, but declined as its port, Ptolemais, grew. It passed to the Ptolemaic Empire in 322 BCE.

blackfoot-confederacy.t: The alliance of the Siksika, Kainai and Piikani, horse-mounted bison hunters who dominated the north-western Plains from the Saskatchewan River to the Missouri.
blackfoot-confederacy.o: The Niitsitapi, Algonquian-speaking peoples of the plains and parklands at the foot of the Rocky Mountains, had long hunted bison on foot. In the early 18th century they acquired horses from the south and guns from Cree middlemen trading with the Hudson's Bay Company, and the Siksika, Kainai and Piikani emerged as an allied military power.
blackfoot-confederacy.r: Each nation was divided into bands led by chiefs chosen for skill in war and generosity, and men's societies policed the summer camps and the communal hunt. Bison provided nearly everything: food, tipis, clothing and tools. The confederacy traded furs at Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company posts but kept American trappers out of its lands for decades. Smallpox epidemics in 1781, 1837 and 1869 killed many.
blackfoot-confederacy.e: After the Marias Massacre of 1870 and the near extinction of the bison, the Blackfoot signed treaties with the United States and, in 1877, Treaty 7 with Canada, negotiated by Crowfoot. Today they live on the Siksika, Kainai and Piikani reserves in Alberta and the Blackfeet Reservation in Montana.

cr.a: Blackfoot Confederacy. "The tipi ring is captured on the Blackfoot Confederacy Flag, designed by Blood Tribe Grandfat...

bhor-state.t: A Maratha state in the Sahyadri hills south of Pune, ruled by the hereditary Pant Sachiv ministers of the Maratha court.
bhor-state.o: Bhor was granted in 1697 to Shankaraji Narayan, appointed Sachiv (minister) by the Maratha king Rajaram. His Deshastha Brahmin family held the office of Pant Sachiv and the lands that supported it.
bhor-state.r: The Pant Sachivs ruled a hilly territory of forts and small farms along the Western Ghats, including Rohida and Rajgad. After 1818 they came under British protection and later the Deccan States Agency. The state introduced some representative institutions before independence.
bhor-state.e: Bhor merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960, in Pune district.

batlokwa-chiefdom.t: The Sotho-speaking Tlokwa chiefdom led by the regent MaNthatisi and her son Sekonyela, a major power and raider during the wars of the 1820s.
batlokwa-chiefdom.o: The Tlokwa were a Sotho-speaking people of the upper Wilge and Caledon river region. When Hlubi and Ngwane refugees broke into the highveld in the early 1820s, the regent MaNthatisi led the Tlokwa on a long series of migrations and raids that made her name feared across the interior, before they settled around the mountain fortresses of Joalaboholo and Marabeng near modern Ficksburg.
batlokwa-chiefdom.r: Power rested on cattle, mountain strongholds and fighting men drawn from many uprooted groups. MaNthatisi handed authority to her son Sekonyela, whose rivalry with Moshoeshoe of the Basotho Kingdom dominated the Caledon valley for two decades. Sekonyela received Wesleyan missionaries but kept to traditional religion, and he clashed in turn with the Voortrekkers, who made him return stolen horses and cattle in 1837.
batlokwa-chiefdom.e: In 1853 Moshoeshoe stormed the Tlokwa strongholds and Sekonyela fled; he died in the Orange Free State. Most of his people were absorbed into the Basotho, while others later settled at Witsieshoek in the Free State, where a Tlokwa chieftaincy survives.

barghawata.t: A Berber confederation on Morocco's Atlantic coast that followed its own prophet and scripture for over three centuries.
barghawata.o: The Barghawata emerged in the Tamesna plain between Salé and Safi after the Berber revolt of 740 against the Umayyad Caliphate. Their first leader, Tarif, took part in the revolt, and around 744 his son Salih ibn Tarif proclaimed himself a prophet, founding a new religion for his people.
barghawata.r: Salih gave the Barghawata a Berber-language scripture of eighty suras and distinct laws, including fasting in the month of Rajab, prayers at different times and food taboos, according to the 11th-century geographer al-Bakri. His successors, such as Yunus ibn Ilyas, spread the faith by force. The confederation of farming and herding tribes fought the Idrisid dynasty, the Banu Ifran emirate and the Caliphate of Córdoba.
barghawata.e: The Almoravid Empire attacked them from 1058; their spiritual leader Abdallah ibn Yasin was killed fighting them in 1059, but the Barghawata were broken. Remnants were finally wiped out by the Almohads in the mid-12th century.

blambangan-kingdom.t: The last Hindu kingdom of Java, on the island's eastern tip, which held out against Muslim Mataram until conquered by the Dutch in 1768.
blambangan-kingdom.o: Blambangan emerged in the eastern salient of Java as a province of Majapahit, and after Majapahit's decline in the 15th and 16th centuries it became an independent Hindu kingdom, with its early capital near Panarukan. Javanese legend remembers its ruler Menak Jingga as the enemy in the Damarwulan story.
blambangan-kingdom.r: Blambangan was a sparsely populated realm of forests and small ports, caught between Muslim Java and Hindu Bali. It fought repeated wars with the Mataram Sultanate and often accepted Balinese protection, especially from Buleleng and Mengwi. In the 17th century Prabu Tawang Alun founded a new capital at Macan Putih.
blambangan-kingdom.e: The Dutch East India Company invaded in 1767 to 1768 to keep out the British, and suppressed the Puputan Bayu rising of 1771 to 1772 with heavy loss of life. The region became Banyuwangi, where the Osing people preserve a distinct language and culture.

batawana-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom of Ngamiland around the Okavango delta, founded by a breakaway branch of the Bangwato.
batawana-chiefdom.o: Around 1795 Tawana, a son of the Bangwato chief, broke away after a succession dispute and led his followers north-west. They eventually settled near Lake Ngami at the edge of the Okavango delta, where they established authority over the BaYei, Hambukushu and other local peoples.
batawana-chiefdom.r: Batawana chiefs ruled from towns near Lake Ngami, drawing tribute in labour and goods from subject peoples. Ngamiland was rich in ivory and ostrich feathers, and the chiefdom traded with Cape and Griqua hunters and merchants. David Livingstone reached Lake Ngami in 1849 during the reign of Letsholathebe I.
batawana-chiefdom.e: Ngamiland was brought into the Bechuanaland Protectorate in the 1880s and 1890s, and the chiefdom continued under colonial rule. Maun became the capital and grew into the main town of north-western Botswana.

billung-march.t: A Saxon frontier march facing the Obotrites along the lower Elbe, held by the Billung family until the great Slavic revolt of 1066.
billung-march.o: Around 936 Otto I entrusted Hermann Billung with command against the Slavs along the lower Elbe, from Holstein to the Peene. This frontier region, later called the Billung March, covered roughly modern Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein, inhabited mainly by Obotrites and other Wendish peoples who paid tribute.
billung-march.r: The march was less a settled territory than a zone of military overlordship and tribute collection. The Billungs, who also became dukes of Saxony, controlled it from strongholds along the Elbe. Bishoprics such as Oldenburg in Holstein were founded to convert the Slavs, but German control remained loose and the Obotrite princes kept considerable power.
billung-march.e: The Great Slav Rising of 983 shook German control, and after the murder of the Christian Obotrite prince Gottschalk in 1066 the Slavs expelled German influence and destroyed churches. The march ceased to exist; German rule returned only with Henry the Lion in the 12th century, leading to the Lordship of Mecklenburg.

bacan-sultanate.t: The southernmost of the four kingdoms of the North Moluccas, on the islands of Bacan south of Halmahera.
bacan-sultanate.o: Bacan was one of the Moloku Kie Raha, the four Moluccan kingdoms with Ternate, Tidore and Jailolo. Its rulers adopted Islam in the late 15th century, like their neighbours, as Javanese and Malay traders sought Moluccan cloves. Local tradition traces the four royal houses to a common ancestor.
bacan-sultanate.r: Bacan was smaller and poorer than Ternate and Tidore but grew cloves and controlled islands to the south and the Obi group. In 1557 its sultan accepted Christianity under Portuguese influence, though later rulers were Muslim. The Dutch built Fort Barneveld on Bacan in the early 17th century, and the sultanate was often a vassal of Ternate.
bacan-sultanate.e: Bacan came under Dutch control in the 19th century and its sultan became a colonial client. After Indonesian independence the sultanate was absorbed into the new state's administration around 1950; the royal family keeps a ceremonial role in North Maluku.

bencoolen.t: British East India Company pepper settlement on the south-west coast of Sumatra, later governed by Stamford Raffles.
bencoolen.o: Expelled from Banten in 1682, the English East India Company sought a new source of pepper and in 1685 founded a post at Bencoolen (Bengkulu) by agreement with local chiefs. It became the Company base in the Malay archipelago, and between 1714 and 1719 the garrison built Fort Marlborough, one of the largest British forts in Asia.
bencoolen.r: The settlement was run by a Company resident and council, later a lieutenant-governor, who forced local farmers to grow pepper for fixed prices. It was unhealthy and lost money for most of its history, and convicts and slaves from India and Africa were used as labour. Thomas Stamford Raffles governed from 1818 to 1824, abolishing slavery and promoting new crops.
bencoolen.e: Under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 Britain exchanged Bencoolen for Dutch Malacca, and the Dutch took over in 1824 and 1825, folding it into the Dutch East Indies. Fort Marlborough still stands in Bengkulu.

bassa-cove.t: A settlement for freed Black Americans on the Liberian coast, founded by Pennsylvania and New York colonisation societies on Quaker principles of peace and temperance.
bassa-cove.o: In 1832 the Young Men's Colonization Society of Pennsylvania, together with the New York colonisation society, founded a settlement at the mouth of the St John river, first called Port Cresson after the Quaker colonisation advocate Elliott Cresson. Its settlers were free Black Americans and emancipated slaves.
bassa-cove.r: The colony was run on Quaker principles: it forbade arms for aggression and banned the sale of alcohol, which also limited its trade with neighbours. In 1835 local Bassa forces, angered by the colony's opposition to the slave trade, destroyed the settlement and killed many settlers. It was refounded as Bassa Cove, and Thomas Buchanan became its governor in 1836.
bassa-cove.e: In 1839 Bassa Cove joined the Colony of Liberia in the Commonwealth of Liberia, with Buchanan as governor of the whole. The town of Buchanan in Grand Bassa County stands near the site.

burgundian-state.t: The patchwork realm of the Valois dukes of Burgundy, from Dijon to the North Sea, whose court set the fashion of 15th-century Europe.
burgundian-state.o: In 1363 John II of France gave the Duchy of Burgundy to his son Philip the Bold. Philip's marriage to Margaret of Male brought Flanders, Artois and the Free County of Burgundy in 1384. His grandson Philip the Good added Namur, Brabant, Holland, Zeeland, Hainaut and Luxembourg between 1421 and 1443.
burgundian-state.r: The dukes held their lands by different titles under France and the Empire and tried to bind them with common institutions, a Chamber of Accounts, the States General from 1464 and the Order of the Golden Fleece, founded in 1430. Flemish and Brabantine towns supplied wealth from cloth and trade, and painters such as Jan van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden worked for the court.
burgundian-state.e: Charles the Bold sought a crown but was killed at Nancy in 1477. Louis XI seized the duchy; Mary of Burgundy married Maximilian of Austria, and after her death in 1482 the Treaty of Arras split the inheritance, the Low Countries passing to the Habsburg Netherlands.

banu-khalid-emirate.t: The Bedouin emirate that ruled eastern Arabia from Hofuf after expelling the Ottomans, until the first Saudi state absorbed it.
banu-khalid-emirate.o: The Banu Khalid were a powerful tribal confederation of eastern Arabia. In 1670 their chief Barrak ibn Ghurayr expelled the Ottoman garrison of the Lahsa Eyalet and made Hofuf the centre of an emirate controlling the coast from Kuwait to Qatar and the oases of al-Hasa and Qatif.
banu-khalid-emirate.r: The emirs governed through tribal alliances, taxing oasis farmers, pearl divers and caravans while keeping nominal ties with the Ottoman Empire. Under their protection, clans of the Bani Utbah settled at Kuwait and later Zubarah in Qatar. Sulayman ibn Muhammad, emir in the mid-18th century, pressured the town of Uyayna to expel the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.
banu-khalid-emirate.e: Family feuds after 1752 weakened the emirate. The Emirate of Diriyah defeated the Banu Khalid in a series of campaigns and conquered al-Hasa by 1796, though the tribe remained important in the region.

balearica.t: The late Roman province of the Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis in the 4th century and lost to the Vandals in 455.
balearica.o: The Balearic Islands, conquered by Rome in 123 BCE, belonged to Hispania Citerior, Tarraconensis and then Carthaginiensis. Around 369 they became a separate province, Balearica, under a governor in the Diocese of Hispania.
balearica.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and trade, with towns such as Palma, Pollentia and on Menorca Mago and Iamo. Christianity was well established by the 5th century. A letter of Bishop Severus of Minorca describes the forced conversion of the Jews of Mago in 418, a rare window on island life.
balearica.e: Vandal raids from Africa struck the islands from 425. Around 455 the Vandals under Gaiseric took control, ending Roman rule. The islands passed to Byzantium after Belisarius' reconquest of Africa in 534.

barony-of-kalavryta.t: Short-lived Frankish barony in the mountains of northern Peloponnese, one of the first lost to the reviving Byzantines.
barony-of-kalavryta.o: Kalavryta was one of the twelve baronies set up in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Otho of Tournay and covered the mountainous district around the town of Kalavryta in the northern Peloponnese, with twelve knight's fiefs.
barony-of-kalavryta.r: Like other baronies, it was held by a French knightly family owing military service and counsel to the prince and governing a Greek peasant population from a castle. Records say little more about it than the name of its lords.
barony-of-kalavryta.e: After the Principality ceded Mistras and other forts to Byzantium in 1262, Byzantine forces pushed north. Kalavryta was taken around 1270 and the barony ceased to exist, though the area later changed hands again before passing permanently to the Despotate of the Morea.

berziti.t: Slavic tribe of western Macedonia, the Brsjaci, caught between Byzantium and Bulgaria until absorbed by the Bulgarian state in the 9th century.
berziti.o: The Berziti were among the Slavic groups that settled in Macedonia in the 7th century, in the region around Ohrid, Prilep and Bitola. Byzantine sources refer to their land as Berzitia; the later Macedonian ethnographic name Brsjaci is often traced to them.
berziti.r: Known only from a few Byzantine notices, they lived under their own chiefs (archons), at times tributary to Byzantium. In the 770s the Bulgarian ruler Telerig planned to resettle them in Bulgaria, and the Byzantine emperor Constantine V campaigned in the region.
berziti.e: During the reigns of Presian and Boris I in the mid-9th century their territory passed to the First Bulgarian Empire, and the name disappears.

belegezites.t: Slavic tribe settled in Thessaly in the 7th century, remembered for trading grain with besieged Thessalonica.
belegezites.o: The Belegezites were one of the Slavic groups that settled in the Balkans during the great migrations of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They occupied lands in Thessaly around Phthiotic Thebes and Demetrias on the Gulf of Volos. Almost everything known about them comes from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, a Byzantine collection of stories about Thessalonica.
belegezites.r: They lived as farming communities under their own chiefs, partly independent of Byzantium. During the Slavic siege of Thessalonica in the 670s they did not join the attackers but sold grain to the starving city, a sign of their prosperity and pragmatic relations with the Byzantines. Their name survives in later Byzantine sources as the region of Velegezitia.
belegezites.e: Over the 8th and 9th centuries Byzantium reasserted control over Greece through the theme system, and the Belegezites were gradually brought under imperial administration, converted to Christianity and absorbed into the Greek-speaking population. They leave few traces apart from place names.
belegezites.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

bengal-sultanate.t: The independent Muslim kingdom that united Bengal for two centuries, nurtured Bengali literature and built the mosques of Gaur and Pandua.
bengal-sultanate.o: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, ruler of Lakhnauti, conquered Satgaon and the Sonargaon Sultanate and in 1352 united Bengal as an independent state. He resisted two invasions by Firuz Shah Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate, securing Bengal's independence, and his Ilyas Shahi dynasty ruled from Pandua and later Gaur.
bengal-sultanate.r: Several dynasties ruled, including the Ilyas Shahis, the line of Raja Ganesha and the Husain Shahis. Bengal exported muslin, silk, rice and sugar through Chittagong, and Chinese envoys of the Ming visited. The sultans patronised Bengali translations of the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Brick mosques such as the Adina Mosque at Pandua and the Sixty Dome Mosque at Bagerhat date from this period.
bengal-sultanate.e: Sher Shah Suri seized Gaur in 1538 and Bengal became part of the Sur Empire. Afghan Karrani rulers then governed it until the Mughal Empire defeated Daud Khan Karrani in 1576. Resistance continued under the Baro-Bhuyans.

beylik-of-the-west.t: The western province of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Mazouna, Mascara and finally Oran, on the frontier with Spain and Morocco.
beylik-of-the-west.o: The Regency of Algiers created the western beylik in 1563, with its first seat at Mazouna. As the Ottomans consolidated control over the former Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen, the capital moved to Mascara around 1700, closer to Spanish Oran, which the beys sought to recapture.
beylik-of-the-west.r: The beys governed the plains and highlands of western Algeria through makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain and livestock. Mustapha Bouchelaghem captured Oran in 1708, though Spain retook it in 1732. Mohammed el-Kebir took possession of Oran in 1792, made it his capital and built mosques there.
beylik-of-the-west.e: After the fall of Algiers in 1830, the last bey, Hassan, surrendered Oran to the French in January 1831. The western tribes soon rallied to the Emirate of Abdelkader, while the territory became part of French Algeria.

burid-emirate-of-damascus.t: The dynasty of Tughtekin that ruled Damascus for half a century, resisting both the Crusaders and the Zengids.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.o: Tughtekin, the Turkish atabeg of the Seljuk prince Duqaq, took power in Damascus after Duqaq's death in 1104. The dynasty takes its name from his son Taj al-Muluk Buri, who succeeded him in 1128.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.r: The Burids governed with the support of the Damascene notables and the urban militia. Tughtekin fought and negotiated with the Kingdom of Jerusalem, while Buri, after the Nizari Ismailis gained influence in the city, allowed a massacre of them in 1129. To resist Zengi of Aleppo, the regent Mu'in al-Din Unur allied with Jerusalem, but the Second Crusade nonetheless besieged Damascus in July 1148 and withdrew after five days.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.e: Weakened by internal rivalries, Mujir al-Din Abaq lost the support of the city, which opened its gates to Nur al-Din in April 1154, uniting Muslim Syria under the Zengid dynasty.

beylik-of-constantine.t: The eastern province of Ottoman Algiers, the largest and richest, whose last bey made Constantine the final stronghold against the French.
beylik-of-constantine.o: The Regency of Algiers organised the eastern beylik in 1567, with its seat in the ancient rock-top city of Constantine. It covered eastern Algeria from Kabylia to the Tunisian border and south to the Saharan oases such as Touggourt.
beylik-of-constantine.r: The beys ruled through local great families and makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain, wool and livestock and paying heavy tribute to Algiers. Salah Bey, who ruled from 1771 to 1792, built mosques, madrasas and bridges and is remembered in local song. Constantine was a centre of learning, crafts and leather work.
beylik-of-constantine.e: After Algiers fell in 1830, Ahmed Bey held Constantine and repulsed a French assault in 1836. The French stormed the city in October 1837, and the beylik was absorbed into French Algeria; Ahmed Bey fought on until 1848.

bishopric-of-pomesania.t: Prussian prince-bishopric on the lower Vistula, closely tied to the Teutonic Order, whose bishop embraced the Reformation in the 1520s.
bishopric-of-pomesania.o: The diocese was one of four created in Prussia by William of Modena in 1243, covering the land of the Pomesanians. The bishop received a third of the territory as his own principality, with the castle of Riesenburg (Prabuty) as residence and a cathedral at Marienwerder (Kwidzyn).
bishopric-of-pomesania.r: Its cathedral chapter belonged to the Teutonic Order from 1285, and the bishops were usually loyal to the Order. Marienwerder became the centre of the cult of Dorothea of Montau, a local mystic. After 1466 the bishopric remained in the Order's part of Prussia, under Polish overlordship.
bishopric-of-pomesania.e: Bishop Erhard von Queis adopted Lutheranism and, after the secularisation of the Order's state into Ducal Prussia in 1525, surrendered his secular rule to Duke Albert in 1527. The territory became part of Ducal Prussia, and the Protestant bishopric was later abolished.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern Andalusia, in modern Granada, Almería and Jaén, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was Basti, near Baza, and they bordered the Oretani, Contestani and coastal Bastuli.
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and Basti, where the Lady of Baza, a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under Rome during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between Hispania Citerior and Baetica in Roman times.

beylik-of-chaka.t: The Aegean emirate of Chaka Bey, the first Turkish ruler to build a fleet and threaten Constantinople from the sea.
beylik-of-chaka.o: Chaka, called Tzachas by the Byzantines, was a Turkish commander who had been a captive at the Byzantine court of Nikephoros III. After his release he seized Smyrna and the Aegean coast of western Anatolia, probably in the late 1080s.
beylik-of-chaka.r: With Greek shipwrights he built a fleet, took Phocaea, Clazomenae and the islands of Lesbos, Chios and Samos, and styled himself emperor. In 1090-1091 he allied with the Pechenegs, who were then besieging Constantinople, but the Byzantine navy and the Pecheneg defeat at Levounion in 1091 ended the threat. Little is known of his government.
beylik-of-chaka.e: Alexios I persuaded Chaka's son-in-law, the Rum Seljuk Kilij Arslan I, to kill him at a banquet around 1093. After the First Crusade, the Byzantine general John Doukas recovered Smyrna in 1097-1098.

bhauma-kara-dynasty.t: A dynasty of coastal Odisha that patronised great Buddhist monasteries and was ruled for long periods by queens.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.o: The Bhauma-Karas came to power in coastal Odisha in the 8th century, replacing the Shailodbhava dynasty. Their capital was Guhadeva-pataka, near modern Jajpur. The dynasty founded an era beginning around 736 that dates their inscriptions.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.r: The early kings were Buddhists who supported monasteries at Ratnagiri, Lalitagiri and Udayagiri; Shubhakara I is thought to be the king of Wu-cha who sent a Buddhist manuscript to the Tang emperor in 795. Later rulers turned to Shaivism. Unusually, several queens ruled in their own right, including Tribhuvana Mahadevi I and Dandi Mahadevi. Temples such as the Vaital Deul in Bhubaneswar date from this period.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.e: After a series of weak rulers the dynasty declined in the 10th century, and the Somavamshi dynasty took over coastal Odisha.

bhopal-state.t: An Afghan-founded Muslim state of central India, famous for its century of rule by four successive women, the Begums of Bhopal.
bhopal-state.o: Dost Mohammad Khan, an Afghan soldier who had served the Mughals, took advantage of imperial decline after 1707 to seize lands in Malwa. He founded Bhopal city and the fort of Fatehgarh, establishing a Muslim dynasty over a largely Hindu population.
bhopal-state.r: Bhopal resisted Maratha pressure and allied with the British in 1818. From 1819 to 1926 four women ruled in turn: Qudsia Begum, Sikandar Begum, Shah Jahan Begum and Sultan Jahan Begum, who built mosques, schools, railways and the Taj-ul-Masajid. It was a nineteen-gun salute state.
bhopal-state.e: Nawab Hamidullah Khan held out against accession until 1949, when Bhopal became a centrally administered state of India. In 1956 it became the capital of Madhya Pradesh.

baraundha-state.t: A small Raghuvanshi Rajput principality in the hills of Bundelkhand, reputed one of the oldest ruling houses of the region.
baraundha-state.o: The ruling family were Raghuvanshi Rajputs who held lands around Patharkachar in the rugged country south of the Yamuna, in what became Bundelkhand. Their traditional history places the founding of the state in the mid-16th century, but details of its early rulers are sparse.
baraundha-state.r: Baraundha was a small, largely rural state of forest and upland villages ruled by a Raja. After British supremacy in Bundelkhand in the early 19th century it was confirmed by sanad and supervised through the Bundelkhand and later Baghelkhand agencies of the Central India Agency.
baraundha-state.e: After Indian independence its ruler acceded to India, and in 1948 Baraundha was merged into the new union of Vindhya Pradesh. Its territory now lies in Satna district of Madhya Pradesh.

bremen-soviet-republic.t: Council republic in the port city of Bremen in early 1919, suppressed after a few weeks by government troops.
bremen-soviet-republic.o: After the November revolution of 1918, workers' and soldiers' councils took power in Bremen. On 10 January 1919, after the Spartacist rising in Berlin, left-wing radicals and Communists proclaimed a Soviet Republic, dissolving the city's senate and parliament.
bremen-soviet-republic.r: The council government, dominated by Communists and Independent Socialists, controlled the city for less than a month. It faced shortages of money and food, as banks refused credit, and opposition from the middle classes and moderate Social Democrats. Its leaders tried to negotiate with the national government but refused to disarm.
bremen-soviet-republic.e: On 4 February 1919 the Freikorps Division Gerstenberg, sent by Gustav Noske, stormed Bremen. About 80 people died, and the Soviet Republic ended. Bremen resumed as a city-state within the Weimar Republic.

barony-of-vostitsa.t: Barony of the Principality of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Vostitsa, the modern Aigio.
barony-of-vostitsa.o: After the Frankish conquest of the Peloponnese, the Principality of Achaea was divided into twelve baronies around 1209. Vostitsa, with a modest number of knight's fiefs, was granted to the Charpigny family from Burgundy, who held it through the 13th century.
barony-of-vostitsa.r: The barons held the castle and town on the south shore of the Gulf of Corinth, owed military service to the prince and sat in his high court, while Greek villagers farmed the land under them. Little detail of daily government survives beyond mentions in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin records.
barony-of-vostitsa.e: In the 14th century the barony passed by inheritance and sale among the Enghien and other lords, and became involved in the struggles of the Navarrese Company. It was eventually lost to the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea in the early 15th century, as the principality crumbled.

belize.t: Central America's only English-speaking country, independent since 1981, home to the world's second-longest barrier reef and a long border dispute with Guatemala.
belize.o: British Honduras was renamed Belize in 1973, and despite Guatemala's claim to the territory it became independent on 21 September 1981 under George Price of the People's United Party, with the British monarch as head of state. British troops stayed to guard it against Guatemala.
belize.r: Power has alternated between the People's United Party and the United Democratic Party, under prime ministers such as Manuel Esquivel, Said Musa, Dean Barrow and Johnny Briceño. Guatemala recognised Belize's independence in 1991, though not its borders, and the British garrison largely left in 1994. Tourism to the reef and Maya sites, sugar, citrus, bananas and seafood support the economy. Its population mixes Kriol, Mestizo, Maya, Garifuna and Mennonite communities.
belize.e: In 2018 and 2019 both Guatemala and Belize voted to submit the territorial dispute to the International Court of Justice, where it remains pending. Belmopan, built after Hurricane Hattie, is the capital, though Belize City is the largest town.

bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.t: An Afghan principality in the Ganges Doab founded by Muhammad Khan Bangash, a soldier of fortune in the late Mughal Empire.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.o: Muhammad Khan Bangash, an Afghan commander who served the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar, was granted lands in the Doab and founded the town of Farrukhabad in 1714, naming it after the emperor. He later served as Mughal governor of Allahabad and Malwa, and built a hereditary principality.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.r: The Bangash nawabs ruled a territory between the Ganges and Yamuna populated by Afghan settlers and Hindu farmers. They fought the Marathas and the Awadh State; Ahmad Khan Bangash defeated an Awadh army in 1750 but was then crushed by a Maratha and Awadh alliance. Farrukhabad became a centre of textile printing and trade.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.e: From the 1770s the nawabs depended on Awadh, and in 1802 Nawab Imdad Husain Khan ceded his territory to the British East India Company in exchange for a pension. The last nawab joined the 1857 rebellion and was exiled.

bangwaketse-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom centred on Kanye whose rulers helped secure British protection rather than Company rule for Botswana.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.o: The Bangwaketse separated from the Bakwena in the 18th century and settled in south-eastern Botswana. Under Makaba II in the late 18th and early 19th centuries they became one of the strongest Tswana states, until Makaba was killed in 1824 during the wars of that era.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled from a large town through ward heads and the kgotla, drawing wealth from cattle and trade in ivory and skins with the Cape. After years of displacement, Gaseitsiwe re-established the chiefdom at Kanye, a defensible hill town. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society were influential.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.e: The chiefdom joined the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. In 1895 Bathoen I travelled to London with Khama III and Sebele I to oppose transfer to the British South Africa Company, and the protectorate was preserved. Ngwaketse is now a district of Botswana.

bagratid-armenia.t: The medieval Armenian kingdom of the Bagratids, whose capital Ani became famous as the city of a thousand and one churches.
bagratid-armenia.o: Ashot Bagratuni, recognised as prince of princes in 862, received a royal crown from the Abbasid caliph around 884 with Byzantine approval, reviving the Armenian monarchy after more than four centuries. The kingdom grew out of the Principality of Armenia and the family's vast estates in Shirak and Ayrarat.
bagratid-armenia.r: The kingdom was a federation of noble houses and rival kingdoms under the Bagratid king of kings. Smbat I was executed by the Sajid emir Yusuf in 914, but Ashot II the Iron restored royal power. Ashot III moved the capital to Ani in 961, which grew wealthy on trade between Byzantium and Iran. Under Gagik I the architect Trdat completed Ani Cathedral in 1001.
bagratid-armenia.e: Hovhannes-Smbat bequeathed his kingdom to Byzantium, and in 1045 Gagik II was forced to surrender Ani to the Byzantine Empire. The Seljuks sacked Ani in 1064, and many Armenians moved west towards Cilicia.

barcid-iberia.t: The Carthaginian domain built in Iberia by Hamilcar Barca and his heirs, the silver-rich base from which Hannibal set out to invade Italy.
barcid-iberia.o: After losing Sicily in the First Punic War, Carthage sent Hamilcar Barca to Iberia in 237 BCE. Landing at Gadir, he conquered the Guadalquivir valley and its mines. After his death in about 229 BCE, his son-in-law Hasdrubal extended Carthaginian power by diplomacy and founded Qart Hadasht, later Carthago Nova, around 227 BCE.
barcid-iberia.r: Barcid Iberia was run almost as a family dominion of the Barcids, nominally under Carthage. Silver from mines near Qart Hadasht and the Sierra Morena paid for armies of Iberian, Celtiberian and African troops. Alliances with local rulers were sealed by marriages, such as Hannibal's to Himilce of Castulo. In 226 BCE the Ebro treaty with Rome fixed a northern limit.
barcid-iberia.e: Hannibal, in command from 221 BCE, took Saguntum in 219 BCE, starting the Second Punic War. Scipio captured Qart Hadasht in 209 BCE and won at Ilipa in 206 BCE, ending Carthaginian rule. The territory became the Roman provinces of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.

barony-of-patras.t: The largest barony of the Principality of Achaea, centred on the port of Patras, later sold to its Latin archbishop.
barony-of-patras.o: When the Principality of Achaea was organised around 1209, Patras, the main port of the north-western Peloponnese, was granted as a barony with 24 knight's fiefs to William Aleman, a knight possibly of German or Provencal origin. He fortified the ancient citadel above the town.
barony-of-patras.r: The barons held the castle and city, owed service to the prince and shared the town with the Latin archbishop, who was the senior Catholic prelate in the principality. Patras was a commercial centre for silk, currants and trade with Italy, with a Greek majority under Latin lords.
barony-of-patras.e: Over the 13th century the archbishops acquired the baronial rights. Around 1276 the barony passed to the archbishop, creating the Latin Archbishopric of Patras, a church-ruled state that lasted until 1430.

bonai-state.t: A hilly princely state on the Brahmani river in northern Odisha, ruled from Bonaigarh until 1948.
bonai-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from the Kadamba dynasty, and tradition dates the state to around 1500. Its early history is poorly documented.
bonai-state.r: Bonai was a rugged, forested state with a largely Adivasi population, including Bhuyan and Munda communities. It was counted among the Chota Nagpur tributary states until 1905, when it was transferred to the Orissa Tributary States. Its hills contain iron ore deposits.
bonai-state.e: Bonai merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now part of Sundargarh district.

bit-adini.t: Bit Adini, an Aramaean kingdom on the Euphrates bend whose fall in 856 BCE opened Syria to Assyrian armies.
bit-adini.o: After the Late Bronze Age collapse, Til Barsip at Tell Ahmar was the Luwian city of Masuwari. In the 10th century BCE Aramaean tribes took control, and the land on both banks of the Euphrates became Bit Adini, the House of Adini, controlling a key river crossing.
bit-adini.r: Bit Adini combined Aramaean tribal leadership with older Luwian urban traditions, and its rulers raised fortified towns. King Ahuni led resistance to Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire, forming alliances with Carchemish and other Syrian kingdoms.
bit-adini.e: Shalmaneser III captured Til Barsip in 856 BCE, renamed it Kar-Shalmaneser and made it an Assyrian base, with palaces decorated with wall paintings. Ahuni was deported to Assyria.

byzantine-spania.t: The East Roman foothold on Spain's south-east coast, won by Justinian in 552 and held for some seventy years against the Visigoths.
byzantine-spania.o: In 552 the Visigothic noble Athanagild, rebelling against King Agila, sought help from Justinian. An imperial force under the elderly patrician Liberius landed in the south-east, and in the following years the Byzantines seized a coastal strip from around Cartagena to Málaga and beyond, organised as the province of Spania.
byzantine-spania.r: Spania was run by a magister militum based at Carthago Nova, and an inscription of 589 records the governor Comenciolus repairing the city's defences. It formed part of Justinian's restoration of the Roman Empire in the West, linked to Byzantine Africa. Its population was Hispano-Roman and Catholic, and Byzantine authority was mainly military and fiscal.
byzantine-spania.e: Visigothic kings steadily pushed the Byzantines back. Leovigild retook inland areas, Sisebut captured Málaga around 615, and Suintila expelled the last imperial forces around 624. Carthago Nova was destroyed in the fighting.

brandenburger-gold-coast.t: Brandenburg-Prussia's short-lived colony on the Gold Coast, centred on the fort of Gross Friedrichsburg near Cape Three Points.
brandenburger-gold-coast.o: The Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg chartered the Brandenburg African Company in 1682, hoping to share in the Atlantic trade. An expedition under Otto Friedrich von der Groeben reached the Ahanta coast and in 1683 founded Gross Friedrichsburg at Pokesu (Princes Town), after treaties with local chiefs. Smaller posts followed at Accada, Takrama and Fort Dorothea.
brandenburger-gold-coast.r: The colony traded guns and cloth for gold, ivory and slaves, many of them shipped to the Danish island of St Thomas in the Caribbean. Its garrisons were tiny and depended on alliances with Ahanta leaders. The company was always short of capital and ships, and Dutch rivals from the Dutch Gold Coast obstructed its trade.
brandenburger-gold-coast.e: King Frederick William I of Prussia, uninterested in overseas ventures, sold the posts to the Dutch in 1717. The Ahanta merchant Jan Conny held Gross Friedrichsburg against them until 1724. The fort, renamed Fort Hollandia, survives as a ruin at Princes Town.

baghal-state.t: A Panwar Rajput hill state of the Simla Hills, ruled from Arki, whose palace holds noted Pahari murals.
baghal-state.o: Baghal was one of the Simla Hill States, ruled by Panwar Rajputs who claimed descent from the Paramaras of Dhar. Rana Sabha Chand founded the capital at Arki in 1643.
baghal-state.r: The Ranas ruled a small hill territory of terraced farms. Gorkha forces from Nepal occupied it from 1803 until the British expelled them in 1815, after which Baghal held a sanad of British protection. The Arki palace is known for its 19th century wall paintings in the Pahari style.
baghal-state.e: Baghal joined the new province of Himachal Pradesh in 1948. Arki is now a town in Solan district.

bruttii.t: Oscan-speaking people who broke away from the Lucanians in 356 BCE and dominated the toe of Italy, Hannibal's last stronghold.
bruttii.o: Diodorus says that in 356 BCE runaway slaves and herdsmen in the mountains of Calabria, then under Lucanian control, rebelled and formed a new people, the Bruttii. The story may simplify a revolt of a subject population, but by the late 4th century BCE they were an independent federation.
bruttii.r: Their capital was Consentia (Cosenza). They lived in hill towns and drew wealth from the Sila forest, producing pitch and timber. They captured Greek cities including Hipponion and Terina and minted fine coins. They fought Alexander of Epirus and joined Pyrrhus against Rome.
bruttii.e: Rome subdued them by 270 BCE and took half the Sila. They joined Hannibal after Cannae, and Bruttium was his last base in Italy until he left in 203 BCE. As punishment they lost land and status; Roman writers said they were reduced to serving as attendants to magistrates.

bazi-dynasty.t: A short Babylonian dynasty of three kings from the house of Bazi, reigning for about twenty years around 1000 BCE.
bazi-dynasty.o: The Bazi Dynasty took its name from Bit-Bazi, a family or tribal group probably of Kassite descent. Its founder, Eulmash-shakin-shumi, became king of Babylon around 1004 BCE after the end of the Second Sealand Dynasty.
bazi-dynasty.r: Very little is known of these reigns beyond king lists and a few chronicle entries and kudurru inscriptions. Eulmash-shakin-shumi ruled for about seventeen years; he was followed briefly by Ninurta-kudurri-usur I and Shirikti-Shuqamuna. Babylonia remained weakened by Aramean settlement and poor harvests, and the kings had limited authority beyond the main cities.
bazi-dynasty.e: Around 985 BCE the dynasty was followed by a single Elamite king, Mar-biti-apla-usur, and then by the Dynasty of E.

bara-kingdom.t: The cattle-herding Bara people of southern-central Madagascar, ruled by Zafimanely nobles in several rival kingdoms.
bara-kingdom.o: The Bara occupied the grasslands of south-central Madagascar around Ihosy, where a ruling house, the Zafimanely, established authority over cattle-herding clans by the 17th century. Tradition links the Zafimanely to the dynasties of the south-east.
bara-kingdom.r: Bara society was organised around cattle, which measured wealth and were central to ritual, and around warrior values, including cattle raiding as a test of manhood. Power was divided among several Zafimanely chiefs rather than a single state. Little written evidence exists before the 19th century.
bara-kingdom.e: The Merina Kingdom established posts in Bara country in the 19th century but never fully controlled it. French forces subdued the region around 1900. The Bara remain one of Madagascar's main pastoral peoples.

british-togoland.t: The western part of German Togoland, ruled by Britain from the Gold Coast, whose 1956 plebiscite made it the first trust territory to join an independent state.
british-togoland.o: Britain and France divided German Togoland in 1916, Britain taking a strip along the western border with the Gold Coast Colony. In 1922 the League of Nations confirmed it as a British mandate, and after 1946 it became a United Nations trust territory. It included part of the Ewe homeland and northern areas linked to Dagbon and Mamprugu.
british-togoland.r: Britain administered the territory as part of the Gold Coast, the north with the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast and the south from the colony, with Ho as the main southern centre. Cocoa farming spread in the south. The division of the Ewe between British Togoland, French Togoland and the Gold Coast fed an Ewe unification movement that petitioned the United Nations.
british-togoland.e: In a UN plebiscite on 9 May 1956 a majority voted for union with the Gold Coast, though most southern Ewe districts voted against. The territory became part of independent Ghana in 1957 as its Volta Region.
