black-sea-soviet-republic.t: A short-lived Soviet republic of 1918 on the Black Sea coast around Novorossiysk, soon merged into the Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic.
black-sea-soviet-republic.o: In March 1918 the Bolsheviks of Black Sea Governorate, a narrow coastal province including Novorossiysk, Tuapse and Sochi, proclaimed the Black Sea Soviet Republic as an autonomous part of the Russian SFSR during the early months of the Civil War.
black-sea-soviet-republic.r: The republic was run by a council of commissars at Novorossiysk, relying on sailors of the Black Sea Fleet and local Red Guards. It struggled with food shortages and with the Georgian advance along the coast towards Sochi, as well as anti-Bolshevik forces. Little is known of its administration.
black-sea-soviet-republic.e: After about two months, in May 1918, it was merged with the Kuban Soviet Republic to form the Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic. The coast passed to the Whites later in 1918, and Soviet rule returned only in 1920.

bilkha-state.t: A small Kathi state near Junagadh, held by a branch of the Vala Kathis of Jetpur.
bilkha-state.o: Bilkha was formed around 1760 as a share of the lands of the Vala Kathis, who also ruled Jetpur State. It was one of many small Kathi holdings in south-central Saurashtra.
bilkha-state.r: Little is recorded about Bilkha beyond its listing as a minor state of the Kathiawar Agency held by Kathi Darbars.
bilkha-state.e: After accession to India Bilkha was merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948; the village is now in Junagadh district of Gujarat.

bailiwick-of-jersey.t: The largest Channel Island, a self-governing Crown Dependency that has stayed loyal to the English crown since the loss of Normandy in 1204.
bailiwick-of-jersey.o: Jersey was part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. After King John lost mainland Normandy in 1204, the island remained with the English crown and became a separate bailiwick under a warden, later a lieutenant governor, with a bailiff heading its Royal Court.
bailiwick-of-jersey.r: Jersey kept Norman customary law and its own States assembly. Mont Orgueil Castle defended it against frequent French attacks. The island traded in cod from Newfoundland, knitted woollens and later potatoes and cattle, and grew into a financial centre. Charles II was proclaimed king there in 1649, and the French were defeated at the Battle of Jersey in 1781.
bailiwick-of-jersey.e: Germany occupied Jersey from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency outside the United Kingdom, with its own parliament, the States Assembly, and its own laws and taxes.

banate-of-severin.t: Hungarian frontier province at the Iron Gates of the Danube, a defensive march against Bulgarians, Cumans and later the Ottomans.
banate-of-severin.o: King Andrew II's son Béla set up the banate around 1228–1233, in lands taken from Bulgaria and the Cumans east of the Iron Gates, around the fortress of Severin (Drobeta-Turnu Severin) built on Roman ruins. In 1247 Béla IV granted it to the Knights Hospitaller, though they soon left.
banate-of-severin.r: A royal ban commanded the castle and the border, collecting tribute from the Romanian voivodes and knezes beyond, such as the Voivodeship of Litovoi. Control shifted repeatedly with Bulgaria and later the Principality of Wallachia, whose rulers took the title ban of Severin. In the 15th century Hungary held it against the Ottomans, and John Hunyadi was ban.
banate-of-severin.e: Ottoman raids steadily wore it down. Severin fortress fell to the Ottomans in 1524, two years before Mohács, and the banate ceased to exist. The region passed to Wallachia as Oltenia's western edge.

british-burma.t: Burma under British rule, built up through three wars from 1824 and governed as part of British India until 1937, then as a separate colony.
british-burma.o: Britain took Arakan and Tenasserim after the First Anglo-Burmese War, settled by the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826. The Second Anglo-Burmese War in 1852 added Lower Burma with Rangoon. In 1885 to 1886 Britain annexed the rest of the Konbaung dynasty's kingdom after the Third Anglo-Burmese War.
british-burma.r: Burma was governed as a province of British India, with Rangoon as its capital. The Irrawaddy delta was cleared for rice, making Burma the world's largest rice exporter, worked by Burman migrants and financed by Indian Chettiar moneylenders. Teak, oil and rubies were exploited. Buddhist associations and students led nationalist protests, and the Saya San rebellion of 1930 to 1932 was suppressed.
british-burma.e: Burma was separated from India in 1937. Japan occupied it from 1942, creating the State of Burma, but Britain returned in 1945. Negotiations with Aung San's Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League led to independence on 4 January 1948 as the Union of Burma.

banu-ifran-emirate.t: A Zenata Berber emirate centred on Tlemcen, born from a Kharijite revolt and later a power in Morocco under Córdoba's overlordship.
banu-ifran-emirate.o: The Banu Ifran were a Zenata Berber tribe of western Algeria. In the great Berber revolt against the Umayyad Caliphate from 740, they embraced Sufri Kharijism, and around 742 their leader Abu Qurra established a state at Tlemcen, where he was proclaimed imam.
banu-ifran-emirate.r: Abu Qurra raised large armies and joined the siege of the Abbasid governor at Tobna in 772. Tlemcen fell to Idris I of the Idrisid dynasty around 790, but the tribe stayed powerful. In the 10th century Ya'la ibn Muhammad founded the town of Ifkan and allied with the Caliphate of Córdoba against the Fatimids. Later Ifranid emirs ruled Salé and Chellah and fought the Barghawata.
banu-ifran-emirate.e: The Almoravid Empire conquered the Ifranid territories in the 1060s, taking Tlemcen and the Moroccan coast, and the tribe was dispersed or absorbed into the new order. Ifranid groups survived in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, where some served as soldiers.

bosporan-kingdom.t: Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
bosporan-kingdom.o: Greek colonies on both sides of the Cimmerian Bosporus, such as Panticapaeum, Phanagoria and Theodosia, united under the Archaeanactid dynasty around 480 BCE. In 438 BCE power passed to Spartocus I, whose Spartocid descendants ruled for more than three centuries from Panticapaeum, modern Kerch, extending control over local Sindians and Maeotians.
bosporan-kingdom.r: The Spartocids called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples. Wealth came from grain, fish and slaves shipped to the Aegean: Leucon I (389-349 BCE) granted Athens tax-free grain purchases and was honoured there. Rich kurgan burials show a blend of Greek and Scythian and Sarmatian culture.
bosporan-kingdom.e: Under pressure from the Scythians, Paerisades V handed the kingdom to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 108 BCE. Later kings, such as Aspurgus and his successors, ruled as clients of Rome. The kingdom declined in the 3rd century CE and was overrun by the Huns in the 370s.
bosporan-kingdom.re: Ancient Greek religion, later also Christianity and Judaism

bhoi-dynasty.t: A short-lived dynasty that took the throne of Odisha after the Gajapatis, whose fall opened the region to the Karrani Afghans.
bhoi-dynasty.o: Govinda Vidyadhara, a minister of the Gajapati Kingdom, killed the last heirs of Prataparudra Deva and seized the throne at Cuttack in 1541. His family, the Bhoi dynasty, inherited a kingdom already reduced by losses to the Vijayanagara Empire and the Golconda Sultanate.
bhoi-dynasty.r: The Bhoi rulers continued the Gajapati title and the royal role in the cult of Jagannath at Puri, but faced constant revolts by nobles and pressure from the Golconda Sultanate and the Afghan rulers of Bengal. Their short reigns were dominated by palace intrigue.
bhoi-dynasty.e: Around 1559 to 1560 the minister Mukunda Deva overthrew the last Bhoi rulers. He was defeated by the Karrani Afghans of Bengal in 1568, ending independent Odisha. Bhoi descendants were later recognised as rajas of the Kingdom of Khurda.

bit-bahiani.t: Bit Bahiani, an Aramaean kingdom of the upper Khabur centred on Guzana, famous for the sculpted palace of King Kapara at Tell Halaf.
bit-bahiani.o: Aramaean tribes took over the upper Khabur in the 10th century BCE, and the House of Bahiani ruled from Guzana, at Tell Halaf on the Syrian-Turkish border. In 894 BCE its king Abi-salamu paid tribute to Adad-nirari II of the Assyrian Empire.
bit-bahiani.r: King Kapara built a palace whose facade had colossal statues of gods on animals and dozens of carved stone reliefs. Excavated by Max von Oppenheim from 1911, they were shattered by bombing in Berlin in 1943 and painstakingly restored. A bilingual statue of the ruler Hadad-yith'i in Assyrian and Aramaic shows the kingdom adapting to Assyrian rule.
bit-bahiani.e: Bit Bahiani became an Assyrian vassal and finally a province c. 808 BCE. Guzana is the Gozan of the Bible, where Israelites were deported after the fall of Samaria.

bibroci.t: British people named only once by Julius Caesar, among the groups that surrendered to him during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
bibroci.o: Known only from Caesar's Gallic War, the Bibroci were one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Cassi, who sent envoys to surrender to him in 54 BCE after the Trinovantes had come under his protection.
bibroci.r: Nothing is recorded of their government, rulers or way of life. Their territory is unknown; scholars have suggested places in the Thames valley or in Berkshire and Sussex, but no inscription or coin securely names them.
bibroci.e: They vanish from the record after Caesar's account. Their land was presumably absorbed by larger neighbours such as the Atrebates (Britain) or the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

baramba-state.t: A small princely state on the Mahanadi in central Odisha, one of the Orissa Tributary States until 1948.
baramba-state.o: Tradition dates the state to the early 14th century, but little is reliably known about its founding.
baramba-state.r: Baramba was a small agricultural state west of Cuttack, known for its handloom weaving. It paid tribute to the Marathas and from 1803 to the British as one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals. Its internal history is poorly recorded.
baramba-state.e: Baramba merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Cuttack district.

basutoland.t: The British territory that preserved Moshoeshoe's mountain kingdom from absorption into South Africa, and became independent Lesotho.
basutoland.o: At Moshoeshoe's request, Britain annexed the Basotho Kingdom in March 1868 to save it from conquest by the Orange Free State, which had already taken much of its lowland farmland. The boundaries were fixed by the Convention of Aliwal North in 1869, and in 1871 the territory was handed to the Cape Colony.
basutoland.r: Cape attempts to disarm the Basotho caused the Gun War of 1880-1881, which the Basotho effectively won, and in 1884 Britain resumed direct rule as a High Commission territory from Maseru. Paramount chiefs of Moshoeshoe's line, among them Letsie I and Lerotholi, kept wide authority, and a Basutoland National Council was created in 1903. Hut tax and poor land made the territory a labour reserve for South African mines.
basutoland.e: Basutoland was never incorporated into South Africa. After the rise of parties such as the Basutoland Congress Party and constitutional reforms, it became independent as the Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966 under Moshoeshoe II.

barolong-chiefdom.t: One of the oldest Tswana chiefdoms, whose branches at Thaba Nchu and Mafikeng were drawn into the struggles between Boers and Britain.
barolong-chiefdom.o: The Barolong are among the oldest Tswana groups, settled in the southern Kalahari margins and the Molopo valley. Under the 18th-century ruler Tau they became a powerful chiefdom, but after his death they split into branches, chief among them the Ratlou, Tshidi, Seleka and Rapulana.
barolong-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns through ward headmen and the kgotla assembly, with cattle herding and cereal farming as the economy. During the wars of the 1820s the Seleka under Moroka moved to Thaba Nchu, where they aided the Voortrekkers in 1836. Methodist missionaries had a strong influence. The Tshidi under Montshiwa settled at Mafikeng and resisted Boer encroachment.
barolong-chiefdom.e: Conflict with the Boer statelets of Stellaland and Goshen led Britain to intervene, and in 1885 Barolong lands were divided between British Bechuanaland and the Bechuanaland Protectorate. Mafikeng later became famous for its siege in the Second Boer War.

banate-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian state ruled by bans under nominal Hungarian overlordship, known for its silver mines and its own Bosnian Church.
banate-of-bosnia.o: Bosnia appears as a distinct land in the 10th century. In 1154 Ban Borić is the first named ruler, a vassal of Hungary. Ban Kulin (c. 1180–1204) made it effectively independent, and his 1189 trade charter to Ragusa is one of the oldest documents in the Serbian-Croatian language.
banate-of-bosnia.r: The ban ruled with a council of nobles from seats around Visoko. The Bosnian Church, an independent church condemned by Rome as heretical, coexisted with Catholicism and Orthodoxy. Under Stephen II Kotromanić (1322–1353) Bosnia annexed Zachlumia and the land up to the Cetina, and Saxon miners opened silver and lead mines at Srebrenica and Fojnica, trading through Ragusa.
banate-of-bosnia.e: In 1377 Ban Tvrtko I had himself crowned king at Mile, claiming the Serbian crown as well, and the banate became the Kingdom of Bosnia.

bhajji-state.t: A small Rajput hill state on the Sutlej north of Shimla, ruled from Seoni, one of the Simla Hill States.
bhajji-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500 and links it to the house of Suket, but little is reliably known of its origins.
bhajji-state.r: Bhajji was a small mountain state above the Sutlej, with its capital at Seoni. It was occupied by the Gurkhas of the Kingdom of Nepal in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
bhajji-state.e: Bhajji merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

banswara-state.t: A Guhila Rajput state in the Vagad hills of southern Rajasthan, created in the 16th century when Dungarpur was divided between two brothers.
banswara-state.o: After Rawal Udai Singh of Dungarpur State was killed at Khanwa in 1527, his lands were divided between his sons. Jagmal Singh took the eastern part across the Mahi river and founded Banswara, named, by tradition, for its bamboo forests.
banswara-state.r: Banswara was a hilly, forested state with a mostly Bhil population, crossed by the Mahi river. Its Maharawals accepted Mughal and then Maratha overlordship and signed a treaty with the British in 1818. The state remained largely rural and poor, with temples and lakes around its capital.
banswara-state.e: Banswara joined the United State of Rajasthan in 1948 and is now a district of Rajasthan, where the Mahi Bajaj Sagar dam was later built.

bit-amukani.t: A Chaldean tribal state of central Babylonia whose leader Nabu-mukin-zeri seized the throne of Babylon in 732 BCE.
bit-amukani.o: Bit-Amukani, 'House of Amukanu', was one of the three main Chaldean tribes that settled in Babylonia in the early first millennium BCE. It held land along the Euphrates in central and southern Babylonia, around the town of Sapia (Shapiya). The Chaldeans first appear in Assyrian annals in the 9th century BCE.
bit-amukani.r: Chaldean tribes were led by sheikhs who controlled walled towns, date groves and trade routes to the Gulf, and they adopted Babylonian names and culture while keeping tribal organisation. In 732 BCE Nabu-mukin-zeri of Bit-Amukani deposed the heir of Nabonassar and became king of Babylon, ending the Dynasty of E.
bit-amukani.e: Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire besieged Sapia and killed Nabu-mukin-zeri in 729 BCE. Bit-Amukani later joined revolts against Assyria, including that of Shamash-shum-ukin, and by the mid-7th century it vanished into Babylonian society.

belize-settlement.t: British logwood and mahogany cutters' settlement on the Bay of Honduras, tolerated by Spain for over a century and the origin of modern Belize.
belize-settlement.o: Tradition dates the first British settlement to 1638 and links it to the buccaneer Peter Wallace, but reliable evidence of logwood cutters, the Baymen, on the Belize River begins in the mid-17th century. Former buccaneers turned to cutting logwood, a valuable dye wood, on a coast Spain claimed but did not occupy.
belize-settlement.r: Spain never recognised British sovereignty but allowed timber cutting under the treaties of Paris in 1763 and Versailles in 1783 and the Convention of London of 1786. The Baymen governed themselves through a Public Meeting and elected magistrates, joined from 1786 by a British superintendent. The economy moved from logwood to mahogany, worked by enslaved Africans in small forest gangs. Settlers repulsed a Spanish attack at the Battle of St George's Caye in 1798.
belize-settlement.e: After Central American independence, Britain extended its control and the settlement's boundaries. Guatemala later claimed the territory, a dispute that still lingers. In 1862 the settlement was formally declared the Colony of British Honduras.

british-military-administration-of-libya.t: British wartime and post-war rule over Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which ended with Libya's UN-sponsored independence in 1951.
british-military-administration-of-libya.o: British Commonwealth forces drove the Axis from Cyrenaica in November 1942 and took Tripoli in January 1943. Britain set up military administrations in both provinces, while France held the Fezzan-Ghadames Military Territory.
british-military-administration-of-libya.r: Under the laws of war, the British largely retained Italian law and administration and many Italian officials, while allowing Libyan political parties to form. The future of the former colony was debated by the victorious powers; in 1949 the Bevin-Sforza plan for trusteeships was rejected by the UN General Assembly.
british-military-administration-of-libya.e: In November 1949 the UN decided that Libya should become independent by 1952, sending Adrian Pelt as commissioner. Cyrenaica became the Emirate of Cyrenaica in 1949, and Libya gained independence as the Kingdom of Libya on 24 December 1951.

bijapur-sultanate.t: The Adil Shahi sultanate of the western Deccan, builder of the Gol Gumbaz, one of the largest domes in the world.
bijapur-sultanate.o: Yusuf Adil Shah, a Bahmani governor of reportedly Turkic or Persian origin, made himself independent at Bijapur around 1490 as the Bahmani Sultanate disintegrated. He briefly held Goa, which was lost to the Portuguese in 1510, and founded a dynasty that dominated the western Deccan for nearly two centuries.
bijapur-sultanate.r: The Adil Shahs alternated between Shia and Sunni allegiance and employed Persian, African and Maratha officers; Shahaji Bhonsle, father of Shivaji, served them. Ibrahim Adil Shah II was a musician and patron of the arts, author of the Kitab-i-Nauras. Bijapur's Ibrahim Rauza and the Gol Gumbaz, tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, are architectural highlights.
bijapur-sultanate.e: Bijapur joined the coalition that defeated the Vijayanagara Empire at Talikota in 1565 and expanded south. Squeezed by the Mughal Empire and the Maratha Kingdom, it fell to Aurangzeb after a long siege in 1686, and the region became a Mughal province.

byeonhan.t: A confederacy of twelve small states on the lower Nakdong river, famed for producing iron that it traded across the Korea Strait and to Chinese commanderies.
byeonhan.o: Byeonhan, also called Byeonjin, took shape in the 1st century BCE in the southeast of the peninsula as one of the three Samhan confederacies, alongside Mahan and Jinhan. Chinese records list twelve member states, sharing customs and language closely with neighbouring Jinhan.
byeonhan.r: Each statelet was ruled by its own chief, with walled settlements and rice and millet farming. Its iron was its great asset: Byeonhan supplied iron to Mahan, Wa in Japan and the Lelang and Daifang commanderies, and iron ingots served as currency. Chinese writers also mention the custom of flattening infants' heads and large bird feathers placed in burials.
byeonhan.e: From the 1st century CE the Byeonhan statelets developed into the Gaya confederacy, traditionally dated to 42 when King Suro founded Geumgwan Gaya at Gimhae. Archaeology shows a gradual change rather than a sharp break.

bakhtiari-confederation.t: A great confederation of Lur nomadic tribes in the Zagros whose khans grew rich from oil and helped win Iran's constitutional revolution.
bakhtiari-confederation.o: The Bakhtiari are Lur tribes who migrate between winter pastures in Khuzestan and summer pastures in the high Zagros. By the 18th century they were organised into two main divisions, the Haft Lang and Chahar Lang, under khans who supplied troops to Safavid, Afsharid and Qajar rulers.
bakhtiari-confederation.r: In 1867 Hossein Qoli Khan was recognised by the Qajar state as ilkhan, paramount chief, unifying the confederation; he was executed in 1882 on the order of Prince Zell-e Soltan. The khans negotiated with British companies over the Lynch road and, after oil was found at Masjed Soleyman in 1908, received shares in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. In 1909 Bakhtiari forces under Sardar As'ad II and Samsam al-Saltaneh marched on Tehran and restored the constitution.
bakhtiari-confederation.e: Reza Shah's Pahlavi Iran disarmed the tribes, forced settlement and executed or imprisoned leading khans by 1934. The Bakhtiari remain a distinct people; Queen Soraya of Pahlavi Iran was of Bakhtiari descent.

bishopric-of-courland.t: Prince-bishopric in western Latvia, founded during the conquest of the Curonians, whose remnant survived as the District of Pilten.
bishopric-of-courland.o: The papal legate Baldwin of Alna created a bishopric for the Curonians in 1234 after treaties with Curonian leaders. When Courland was conquered by the Livonian Order in the 1250s and 1260s, the bishop received about a third of the land, scattered in several districts.
bishopric-of-courland.r: The bishop's lands centred on Pilten and Hasenpoth, with the cathedral at Hasenpoth (Aizpute). Unlike other Livonian bishops, those of Courland were closely tied to the Livonian Order, and the chapter was for a time made up of Order priests. Curonian and Latvian peasants worked the estates of German vassals.
bishopric-of-courland.e: In 1559 Bishop Johann von Münchhausen sold the bishopric to Frederick II of Denmark, who gave it to his brother Magnus of Holstein. After Magnus died in 1583, Denmark sold its rights to Poland-Lithuania in 1585, and the territory became the District of Pilten.

barotseland.t: The Lozi kingdom of the upper Zambezi floodplain, ruled by the Litunga, which kept a special status under British rule until Zambian independence.
barotseland.o: The Luyi (later Lozi) people settled the Bulozi floodplain of the upper Zambezi, with traditions linking their first ruler, Mbuyu, to the Lunda world. By the 17th century the Litunga headed a centralised kingdom that drew on the floodplain's fish, cattle and cultivated mounds.
barotseland.r: The Litunga ruled through a council (kuta) of titled officials and a system of state-owned labour and tribute, and moved his court each year from the flooding plain to higher ground in the Kuomboka ceremony. Mulambwa reformed the law in the early 19th century. From about 1840 the kingdom was conquered by the Makololo under Sebitwane, but Sipopa restored Lozi rule in 1864.
barotseland.e: Lewanika signed a concession with the British South Africa Company in 1890, and Barotseland became a protectorate within Northern Rhodesia with its own institutions. The 1964 Barotseland Agreement merged it into independent Zambia, a settlement still disputed today.

belgian-congo.t: Belgium's vast central African colony, a paternalistic mining economy whose hasty independence in 1960 led to the Congo Crisis.
belgian-congo.o: After international outrage over abuses in the Congo Free State, the Belgian parliament annexed King Leopold II's personal domain on 15 November 1908. A Colonial Charter placed it under the Belgian government, with a governor-general at Boma.
belgian-congo.r: Rule rested on the state, the Catholic missions and large companies, the so-called colonial trinity. Union Minière du Haut Katanga mined copper and cobalt, and uranium from Shinkolobwe supplied the Manhattan Project. Primary schooling and health care spread widely, but Africans were barred from higher posts and university until the 1950s. Simon Kimbangu's prophetic church was repressed. The capital moved to Léopoldville in the 1920s.
belgian-congo.e: Riots in Léopoldville in 1959 led Belgium to grant independence on 30 June 1960, with Joseph Kasavubu as president and Patrice Lumumba as prime minister. Mutiny and the secession of Katanga followed within days.

barony-of-chalandritsa.t: Small Frankish barony in the hills south of Patras, one of the original fiefs of the Principality of Achaea.
barony-of-chalandritsa.o: Chalandritsa was among the baronies created in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Robert de la Tremouille, a knight from France, and held a small number of knight's fiefs in the hill country of Achaea south of Patras.
barony-of-chalandritsa.r: The barons owed military service to the prince and had seats in his high court. The Dramelay family later held it for much of the 13th and 14th centuries. Beyond these facts, recorded in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin documents, little is known of the barony's internal life.
barony-of-chalandritsa.e: In the final collapse of the principality, Chalandritsa was taken by the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea, under Constantine Palaiologos, in 1429, at the same time as the campaign that won Patras.

buton-sultanate.t: An island sultanate off southeast Sulawesi, known for its massive Wolio fortress and an unusual elected monarchy that lasted until 1960.
buton-sultanate.o: Buton's chronicles trace its kingdom to the 14th century and a legendary first queen, Wa Kaa Kaa. Placed on the sea route between Java, Makassar and the Moluccas, it grew as a port and a power over the nearby islands. Its sixth king, Lakilaponto, adopted Islam around 1540 and became Sultan Murhum.
buton-sultanate.r: Buton was governed by a written constitution, the Martabat Tujuh, adopted under Sultan La Elangi in the early 17th century and inspired by Sufi thought. Sultans were elected by a council of nobles from rotating royal houses and could be deposed. The Wolio fortress, with walls nearly three kilometres long, protected the capital.
buton-sultanate.e: Squeezed between Gowa and Ternate, Buton allied with the Dutch East India Company from 1613. It kept internal autonomy under Dutch rule. After the death of the last sultan, Muhammad Falihi Kaimuddin, in 1960, the sultanate ended and its lands became regencies of Southeast Sulawesi.

borno-emirate.t: The Kanuri emirate under British rule that continued the ancient Kanem-Bornu monarchy from its new capital at Maiduguri.
borno-emirate.o: After Rabih az-Zubayr was killed in 1900, the French and British restored the al-Kanemi dynasty, rulers of the Kanem-Bornu Empire since the early 19th century. In 1902 Shehu Abubakar Garbai moved into British territory and was recognised as ruler of the British part of Bornu. In 1907 he founded a new capital at Yerwa, which grew into the city of Maiduguri.
borno-emirate.r: Under indirect rule the shehu governed through district heads and Islamic courts, supervised by British officials of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria and later Colonial Nigeria. The emirate kept Bornu's court titles and its tradition as a centre of Islamic scholarship. Its economy rested on farming, cattle and trade across Lake Chad. Shehu Umar Sanda Kyarimi reigned from 1937 to 1968.
borno-emirate.e: With Nigerian independence in 1960 the emirate became part of the Northern Region and later of Borno State. The Shehu of Borno remains one of the most senior traditional rulers in Nigeria.

bourbon-restoration.t: The return of the Bourbon kings after Napoleon, a constitutional monarchy under Louis XVIII and Charles X that ended in the July Revolution of 1830.
bourbon-restoration.o: After Napoleon's abdication in April 1814 the allies and the French Senate restored Louis XVIII, brother of Louis XVI. He granted the Charter of 1814, which kept a parliament and many revolutionary gains. Napoleon's return in the Hundred Days of 1815 interrupted the regime until Waterloo.
bourbon-restoration.r: France had a two-chamber parliament elected by a very small, wealthy electorate. Moderate ministers such as the Duke of Richelieu paid off war indemnities and ended the allied occupation in 1818, while ultra-royalists pressed for revenge after the White Terror. Charles X, crowned at Reims in 1825, compensated émigrés and favoured the Church.
bourbon-restoration.e: In July 1830 Charles X issued ordinances dissolving parliament and curbing the press. Three days of revolt in Paris drove him into exile, and Louis-Philippe of Orléans became king, beginning the July Monarchy. Algiers had been taken weeks earlier.

bonny-kingdom.t: Ijaw trading state of the eastern Niger delta, one of the busiest slave ports of the 18th century and then a centre of the palm oil trade.
bonny-kingdom.o: Bonny, called Ibani by its people, was founded by Ijaw migrants on an island near the mouth of the Bonny river, traditionally in the 15th century. By the 17th century it was dealing with Portuguese, Dutch and English ships, buying captives from the Igbo hinterland through networks such as the Aro Confederacy.
bonny-kingdom.r: The Amanyanabo ruled with the heads of trading houses, which absorbed slaves and could be led by able former slaves. The Pepple dynasty, founded by Perekule in the 18th century, presided over a huge slave trade and then a shift to palm oil after abolition. The British consul deposed King William Dappa Pepple in 1854.
bonny-kingdom.e: In 1869 the former slave and house head Jaja left Bonny to found the Kingdom of Opobo, taking much of its trade. Bonny signed a British protection treaty in 1884 and became part of the Oil Rivers Protectorate. It is now a key oil and gas terminal.

bikaner-state.t: The Rathore desert kingdom of northern Rajasthan, founded by a son of Rao Jodha, whose 20th-century Maharaja turned it green with the Ganga Canal.
bikaner-state.o: In 1465 Rao Bika, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, led followers north into the Jangladesh region of the Thar and carved out a kingdom from local Jat and Bhati lands. He founded the city of Bikaner in 1488.
bikaner-state.r: Raja Rai Singh served Akbar as a general and built the Junagarh fort. Bikaner traded across the desert and was home to many Marwari merchant families. Maharaja Ganga Singh (r. 1887–1943) raised the Ganga Risala camel corps, sat in the Imperial War Cabinet during the First World War and built the Ganga Canal, opened in 1927 to irrigate the north of the state.
bikaner-state.e: Bikaner signed a treaty with the British in 1818 and acceded to India in 1947. It merged into Greater Rajasthan in 1949 and is now a district of Rajasthan.

banu-qasi.t: A Muslim dynasty of Visigothic descent that dominated the upper Ebro for two centuries, allied by blood with the kings of Pamplona.
banu-qasi.o: The Banu Qasi claimed descent from a Visigothic count called Cassius who converted to Islam after the conquest of 711 to 714, keeping his lands in the upper Ebro valley. As muwallads, native Muslims, they became the leading family of the Upper March, based at Tudela.
banu-qasi.r: They balanced between Córdoba, the Franks and the Christian kingdoms, intermarrying with the Arista family of Pamplona, whose founder Íñigo Arista was a half-brother of Musa ibn Musa. Musa ruled Tudela, Zaragoza and Huesca and was called the third king of Spain, until Ordoño I of Asturias defeated him at Albelda in 859. Later family members fought Córdoba, the Tujibids and Navarre.
banu-qasi.e: Weakened by family divisions and wars with Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona, the dynasty lost Tudela and its lands. Abd al-Rahman III ended its power in the 920s, and the Tujibid family took over the Upper March.

brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.t: The last Hindu dynasty of Sindh, whose king Dahir fell in 712 to the Arab army of Muhammad ibn Qasim.
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.o: According to the Chach Nama, a 13th-century Persian history, Chach, a Brahmin chamberlain at the court of the Rai dynasty, married the widowed queen after the death of Rai Sahasi II and seized the throne at Aror around 632. He spent his reign subduing rebellious governors and fixing the borders of Sindh.
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.r: The Chach Nama describes a kingdom divided into provinces under governors, with a strong Buddhist population, many monasteries and powerful Jat and Lohana groups in the countryside. Chach was succeeded by his brother Chandar and then by his sons, of whom Dahir ruled from Aror while his brother held Brahmanabad. Sindh's ports, such as Debal, were active in Indian Ocean trade.
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.e: After attacks on Arab ships near Debal, the Umayyad governor of Iraq, al-Hajjaj, sent Muhammad ibn Qasim, who took Debal in 711 and defeated and killed Dahir in 712. Sindh became a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, and later the Habbari dynasty and the Emirate of Multan arose there.

banu-khattab-emirate.t: A Berber Ibadi dynasty of the Fezzan, ruling the Saharan slave-trade town of Zawila for over two centuries.
banu-khattab-emirate.o: Zawila, in the Fezzan of southern Libya, lay in the former lands of the Garamantian Empire. Around 918 Abd Allah ibn al-Khattab of the Hawwara Berbers established the dynasty there, controlling oases on the main caravan route between Lake Chad and the Mediterranean.
banu-khattab-emirate.r: The Banu Khattab were Ibadi Muslims who ruled a network of oases from Zawila, which Arab geographers describe as a walled town with a mosque and markets. The emirate grew rich from the trade in enslaved people brought from Kanem and the Lake Chad region, exchanged for horses, textiles and metal goods, and from date cultivation.
banu-khattab-emirate.e: In 1172 to 1176 Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush, a commander serving the Ayyubid Empire of Saladin, invaded the Fezzan and killed the last Khattabid ruler. The Fezzan later came under Kanem and local dynasties.

balaton-principality.t: Frankish vassal principality around Lake Balaton where Pribina and Kocel built churches and welcomed Methodius's Slavonic liturgy.
balaton-principality.o: Pribina, a Slavic prince expelled from Nitra by Mojmir I of Moravia around 833, entered Frankish service. Around 839 Louis the German granted him lands in Lower Pannonia, and he built a fortified seat at Mosapurc (Zalavár) on the Zala river near Lake Balaton.
balaton-principality.r: Pribina ruled as a Frankish vassal, settling Slavs and Bavarians and founding some 30 churches consecrated by the archbishops of Salzburg. Under his son Kocel, Mosapurc was an important church centre. In 867 Kocel welcomed Cyril and Methodius and supported the Slavonic liturgy, and Methodius was made archbishop of Pannonia in 870.
balaton-principality.e: Pribina was killed fighting Moravians in 861. After Kocel's death around 876 the principality returned to direct Frankish rule, and the Hungarian conquest of the 890s ended Frankish power in Pannonia.

british-seychelles.t: The Indian Ocean archipelago held by Britain from the Napoleonic Wars until 1976, a plantation colony and a place of exile.
british-seychelles.o: The French-settled Seychelles surrendered to British warships several times during the Napoleonic Wars, while the French commandant Quéau de Quinssy stayed on to run the islands. After the capture of Mauritius in 1810 they passed under British control, confirmed by the Treaty of Paris in 1814, and were governed as a dependency of Mauritius.
british-seychelles.r: French-speaking planters grew cotton and then coconuts, cinnamon and vanilla with enslaved labour until abolition in 1835; Africans freed from slave ships by the Royal Navy were later landed there. A Creole society formed, mostly Catholic. The islands became a separate Crown colony in 1903 with its capital at Victoria, and served as a place of exile for figures such as Prempeh I of Asante and Archbishop Makarios of Cyprus.
british-seychelles.e: After internal self-government in 1970, the Seychelles became independent on 29 June 1976 as a republic within the Commonwealth under President James Mancham, whose government was overthrown in a coup the next year by France-Albert René.

brigantes-ireland.t: People of south-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, bearing the same name as the great Brigantes confederation of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 lists the Brigantes in south-eastern Ireland, usually placed in the area of modern Wexford and Waterford, near the Coriondi and the Usdiae. The name, meaning roughly 'the high ones' or linked to the goddess Brigantia, is the same as that of the Brigantes of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. The shared name has encouraged theories of migration from Britain to Ireland, or of a common cult of a goddess later remembered as Brigit, but there is no evidence beyond the name. The south-east coast faced Wales and Gaul and was open to sea trade.
brigantes-ireland.e: The Irish Brigantes vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Leinster, the Kingdom of Osraige and the lands of the Deisi Muman.

baban-emirate.t: A Kurdish emirate that founded the city of Sulaymaniyah and became a cradle of Sorani Kurdish literature between the Ottoman and Persian empires.
baban-emirate.o: The Baban family rose in the mountains of Shahrizor in the 17th century, recognised by the Ottoman Empire as hereditary lords. Their early centre was Qalacholan. In 1784 Ibrahim Pasha Baban founded Sulaymaniyah, named after the Mamluk governor of Baghdad, Büyük Süleyman Pasha, as his new capital.
baban-emirate.r: The emirate was a frontier state caught between Mamluk Iraq and Qajar Iran, each of which tried to choose its emirs; family members often appealed to one side against the other. Sulaymaniyah became a centre of learning, where poets such as Nali, Salim and Kurdi wrote in Sorani Kurdish rather than Persian, founding a new literary tradition. The economy rested on agriculture, livestock and trade between Baghdad and Persia.
baban-emirate.e: As the Ottomans centralised, they deposed the last emir, Ahmad Pasha, in 1850 and placed the region under a governor. The family remained influential in Kurdish politics.

buyid-dynasty.t: Daylamite Shia rulers who controlled the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and most of Iran for over a century, the high point of the 'Iranian intermezzo'.
buyid-dynasty.o: Three sons of Buya, a Daylamite of modest origin, rose as officers under Mardavij of the Ziyarid dynasty. In 934 Ali took Fars and made Shiraz his base; his brothers Hasan took Ray and Isfahan, and Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945. The caliph gave them the titles Imad al-Dawla, Rukn al-Dawla and Mu'izz al-Dawla.
buyid-dynasty.r: The Buyids kept Sunni Abbasid caliphs as figureheads while ruling as emirs and later as shahanshah, a revived Persian title. They were Shia and sponsored public Ashura mourning and the feast of Ghadir in Baghdad. Adud al-Dawla, who united the realm in 977 to 983, built the Band-e Amir dam in Fars and the Adudi hospital in Baghdad. Their courts patronised scholars such as Miskawayh and the vizier al-Sahib ibn Abbad, and they spread the iqta land-grant system.
buyid-dynasty.e: Family rivalries split the state. Mahmud of the Ghaznavid Empire took Ray in 1029, and Tughril of the Seljuk Empire entered Baghdad in 1055. The last Buyid in Fars was overthrown by the Shabankara chief Fadluya in 1062.

bahamas.t: Archipelago of some 700 islands off Florida, independent since 1973 and one of the wealthiest Caribbean states through tourism and finance.
bahamas.o: After winning majority rule in 1967, Lynden Pindling's Progressive Liberal Party led the Colony of the Bahamas to independence on 10 July 1973 as the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, a parliamentary monarchy with the British monarch as head of state.
bahamas.r: Pindling, called the father of the nation, governed until 1992, expanding education and Bahamian ownership, though his government was tarnished by drug trafficking scandals in the 1980s, when the islands served as a transit route for cocaine to the United States. Hubert Ingraham's Free National Movement then alternated in power with the Progressive Liberal Party. Tourism, especially cruise and resort tourism on New Providence and Grand Bahama, and offshore banking dominate the economy.
bahamas.e: The Bahamas remains a stable parliamentary democracy. Hurricane Dorian devastated Abaco and Grand Bahama in 2019, and rising sea levels threaten the low-lying islands. Philip Davis became prime minister in 2021.

bahawalpur-state.t: The Abbasi Nawabs' desert kingdom along the Sutlej, the largest princely state to join Pakistan.
bahawalpur-state.o: The Daudpota Abbasi clan, who claimed descent from the Abbasid caliphs, moved from Sindh to the Sutlej valley in the early 18th century. Around 1748 Bahawal Khan I founded the town of Bahawalpur, and the Nawabs became independent of the declining Durrani Empire.
bahawalpur-state.r: The Nawabs signed a treaty with the British in 1833 and supported them in the Afghan and Anglo-Sikh wars and in 1857. Much of the state was Cholistan desert, but the Sutlej Valley Project of the 1920s greatly expanded irrigated farming. The Nawabs built palaces such as Noor Mahal and held the old fort of Derawar.
bahawalpur-state.e: Sadiq Muhammad Khan V acceded to Pakistan in October 1947 and gave the new state generous financial support. Bahawalpur was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and is now a division of Punjab province.

beikthano.t: One of the oldest Pyu cities in Myanmar, whose name means 'Vishnu city' and whose excavated monastery and burials show early contact with India.
beikthano.o: Beikthano grew up in the Magway region of central Myanmar from around the 2nd century BCE, making it among the earliest walled cities of the Pyu. Radiocarbon dates from excavations in the 1950s and 1960s place its main occupation between about 200 BCE and 400 CE.
beikthano.r: The city was enclosed by a roughly rectangular brick wall about 3 km long, with irrigation works feeding rice fields around it. Excavators found a palace site, a monastery and stupa resembling those of Nagarjunakonda in south India, and many burial urns holding cremated remains, suggesting early Buddhist practice alongside local customs.
beikthano.e: Beikthano was abandoned or declined around the 4th or 5th century, possibly after a fire, as Sri Ksetra rose as the leading Pyu centre. Local legend links its end to a princess named Panhtwa. It is now one of the three Pyu ancient cities on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

bahdinan-emirate.t: A Kurdish emirate in the mountains north of Mosul, centred on the clifftop town of Amadiya, that ruled for over four centuries.
bahdinan-emirate.o: The Bahdinan emirs claimed descent from the Abbasid caliphs through an ancestor named Baha al-Din, who gave the dynasty its name. They ruled from Amadiya (Amedi), a town on a sheer rock plateau in the mountains of northern Iraq, from at least the late 14th century.
bahdinan-emirate.r: The emirs governed Kurdish tribes, Assyrian Christian and Jewish villages and Yazidi communities in the valleys between the Great Zab and the Khabur. After the Ottoman conquest of the region in the 16th century they became hereditary vassals of the Ottoman Empire, providing troops for its wars with the Safavids; Sultan Husayn Wali was a notable ally of the Ottomans. Amadiya was known for its madrasas and its Sunni scholars.
bahdinan-emirate.e: Weakened by internal feuds and attacks by the Soran emirate in the 1830s, the emirate was abolished during Ottoman centralisation in the early 1840s, its lands placed under the governor of Mosul.

banat-of-temeswar.t: Habsburg crown domain in the plain of the Banat, run directly from Vienna as a laboratory of colonisation and drainage after its conquest from the Ottomans.
banat-of-temeswar.o: Prince Eugene of Savoy captured Temeswar from the Ottomans in 1716, and the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 confirmed Habsburg possession of the Banat between the Mureș, Tisza and Danube. Rather than returning it to Hungary, Charles VI kept it as a crown domain under military and court administration.
banat-of-temeswar.r: Governor Claudius Florimund Mercy rebuilt Temeswar as a baroque fortress town, drained marshes, dug the Bega canal and promoted rice, silk and mining. Tens of thousands of Catholic German settlers, later called Danube Swabians, were brought in alongside Serbs, Romanians and Italians, while Hungarian nobles were largely excluded. The Banat was governed by a provincial administration answering to Vienna.
banat-of-temeswar.e: In 1778 Maria Theresa returned the civil Banat to Hungary as the counties of Temes, Torontál and Krassó, while its southern strip stayed in the Military Frontier. Its mixed population shaped the region until it was divided between Romania, Yugoslavia and Hungary in 1920.

balhae.t: A kingdom of Manchuria and northern Korea founded by Goguryeo and Mohe people, so prosperous that Tang China called it the flourishing land of the east.
balhae.o: After the fall of Goguryeo, Dae Joyeong led Goguryeo refugees and Mohe tribesmen out of Tang-controlled Liaoxi, defeated a Tang army at Tianmenling and in 698 founded the state of Jin near the Dongmo mountain. In 713 Tang recognised him as king of Bohai, the name by which the state became known.
balhae.r: Balhae copied Tang institutions, with three departments and six ministries, five capitals and fifteen prefectures, while its kings sometimes used their own era names. King Mun moved the court to Sanggyeong, laid out on the plan of Chang'an. Its elite wrote Chinese and practised Buddhism, and some thirty-four embassies to Japan carried furs, honey and ginseng.
balhae.e: Weakened by internal conflict, Balhae fell in 926 to the Khitan under Abaoji, who made it the vassal kingdom of Dongdan. Many nobles fled to Goryeo, which welcomed the crown prince Dae Gwang-hyeon.

bharatpur-state.t: The Jat kingdom of eastern Rajasthan whose mud-walled fortress of Lohagarh famously withstood a British siege in 1805.
bharatpur-state.o: Jat peasant leaders around Mathura and Agra rose against Mughal authority in the late 17th century. Badan Singh, recognised as chief around 1722, consolidated the clans and fortified Deeg and Bharatpur. His son Suraj Mal (ruled 1755–63) turned the chiefship into a major power, building the Lohagarh fort and capturing Agra in 1761.
bharatpur-state.r: Bharatpur was a Hindu Jat monarchy with a strong military tradition and a wealthy farming base. Its forts at Bharatpur and Deeg, with the Deeg water palaces, reflect Suraj Mal's ambitions. In 1805 Lord Lake failed to take Lohagarh after four assaults; the fort finally fell to Lord Combermere in 1826, after which Bharatpur was a British protected state. The Keoladeo wetlands were kept as a royal duck-shooting reserve.
bharatpur-state.e: After independence Bharatpur joined the Matsya Union in March 1948, which merged into the United State of Rajasthan in 1949. Keoladeo is now a national park and World Heritage Site.

bourbon-spain.t: Spain under the Bourbon dynasty from Philip V to Isabella II, a time of centralising reform, Napoleonic invasion and the loss of most of its American empire.
bourbon-spain.o: Charles II, last of Habsburg Spain, left the throne to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV, who became Philip V in 1700. The War of the Spanish Succession confirmed him as king but cost Spain its European possessions at Utrecht in 1713, while the Nueva Planta decrees abolished the separate institutions of the Crown of Aragon.
bourbon-spain.r: The Bourbons built a more centralised state on the French model, with intendants, new academies and royal factories. Charles III (1759-1788) promoted roads, trade reform and enlightened ministers and expelled the Jesuits. The monarchy was shattered by the 1808 French invasion; Ferdinand VII then restored absolutism, and the American colonies won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.
bourbon-spain.e: Isabella II's reign was dominated by Carlist Wars, generals and court scandal. The Glorious Revolution of September 1868 drove her into exile, opening the Sexenio Democrático.

broerec.t: Breton kingdom of the Vannes region, named the land of Waroch after a warlord who defied the Franks.
broerec.o: In the 6th century Breton rulers extended their power over the Vannetais, the former land of the Veneti, which remained largely Gallo-Roman. Gregory of Tours records the counts Macliau and his son Waroch fighting for control of Vannes.
broerec.r: Waroch repeatedly raided Frankish territory around Rennes and Nantes and defeated or bought off Frankish armies sent by Guntram and Chilperic I in the 570s and 580s. The region kept a strong Gallo-Roman element alongside the Breton settlers, and Vannes remained a bishopric.
broerec.e: Broërec remained the border zone between the Bretons and the Franks until it was absorbed into the Kingdom of Brittany created by Nominoe, who was count of Vannes for Louis the Pious. Its name survives in the Breton name of the Vannes region.

bishopric-of-dorpat.t: Prince-bishopric of south-eastern Estonia centred on Dorpat (Tartu), a prosperous Hanseatic frontier facing Pskov, until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1558.
bishopric-of-dorpat.o: Hermann of Buxhoeveden, brother of Bishop Albert of Riga, became bishop of the Estonians in 1220 and moved his see to Dorpat after its capture in 1224. The bishopric took over the former lands of Ugandi, Vaiga and Mõhu, and Hermann received them as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire.
bishopric-of-dorpat.r: The bishop ruled through a cathedral chapter and German vassals, sharing power with the Livonian Order and the diets of Terra Mariana. Dorpat, a Hanseatic member, grew rich from trade with Pskov and Novgorod and built a large Gothic cathedral. Estonian peasants worked the land under increasing serfdom.
bishopric-of-dorpat.e: At the start of the Livonian War Ivan IV of Russia took Dorpat in 1558, and the last bishop, Hermann Wesel, was taken to Russia, where he died. The territory was later contested by Poland-Lithuania and Sweden, and passed to Swedish Livonia in the 1620s.

bavda-state.t: A Maratha jagir in the Western Ghats under Kolhapur, held by the hereditary Pant Amatya family.
bavda-state.o: Bavda (Gaganbawada) was held by the descendants of Ramchandra Pant Amatya, the minister who defended the Maratha kingdom during the war with Aurangzeb in the 1690s. Around 1700 the family received this hill territory with the hereditary title of Pant Amatya, as feudatories of Kolhapur.
bavda-state.r: The chiefs governed a hilly, forested territory on the Ghats overlooking the Konkan, under Kolhapur overlordship and British supervision through the Kolhapur residency. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
bavda-state.e: Bavda merged with Kolhapur into Bombay Province in 1949 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. Gaganbawada is a taluka of Kolhapur district.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the Jalón and Huerva valleys of modern Zaragoza province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included Segeda and Contrebia Belaisca, the modern Botorrita.
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The Botorrita bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from Contrebia Belaisca and record local regulations, while a Latin bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE Segeda enlarged its walls, which Rome treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by Carus of Segeda, the Celtiberians defeated the consul Nobilior, but after Numantia fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

bauchi-emirate.t: A large emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate in north-central Nigeria, unusual in having been founded by a non-Fulani flag-bearer, Yakubu.
bauchi-emirate.o: Yakubu, a Gerawa scholar and student of Usman dan Fodio, was the only one of the original flag-bearers who was not a Fulani. Receiving a flag around 1805, he campaigned among the many peoples of the Jos plateau foothills and the upper Gongola, and around 1809 founded the town of Bauchi as his capital.
bauchi-emirate.r: Yakubu ruled for about forty years and built one of the larger emirates by conquering and raiding many small non-Muslim groups, whose captives supplied slaves for farms and trade. The emirate was governed by the emir with titled officials and sub-emirates on its frontiers, and owed allegiance and tribute to Sokoto. Its southern borderlands remained contested hill country throughout the century.
bauchi-emirate.e: British forces occupied Bauchi in 1902 and deposed the reigning emir, and the emirate became part of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria. The Emir of Bauchi continues as a traditional ruler in modern Bauchi State.

bulgaria.t: Present-day Bulgaria, a parliamentary republic since 1990 and member of NATO and the European Union.
bulgaria.o: After Todor Zhivkov's fall in November 1989 ended the dominance of the People's Republic of Bulgaria's communist party, Round Table talks led to free elections in 1990. The country was renamed the Republic of Bulgaria in November 1990, and a democratic constitution was adopted in July 1991. The philosopher Zhelyu Zhelev became the first directly elected president.
bulgaria.r: Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic with a single-chamber National Assembly. The transition was painful: a banking collapse and hyperinflation in 1996 to 1997 led to a currency board pegging the lev. The former tsar Simeon II became prime minister in 2001 as Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. Corruption and weak institutions remain central political issues.
bulgaria.e: Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. Boyko Borisov dominated politics from 2009 until mass protests in 2020, followed by repeated snap elections. The country fully joined the Schengen area in 2025 and adopted the euro in 2026.

bavarian-soviet-republic.t: Short-lived council republic in Munich in April 1919, crushed by government troops and Freikorps in a wave of violence.
bavarian-soviet-republic.o: After the murder of Bavarian premier Kurt Eisner in February 1919, the elected government of Johannes Hoffmann fled Munich to Bamberg. On 6-7 April 1919 a council republic was proclaimed by writers and anarchists, including Ernst Toller, Erich Mühsam and Gustav Landauer.
bavarian-soviet-republic.r: The first council government was chaotic; within a week the Communists under Eugen Leviné took over and formed a Red Army. They decreed the socialisation of banks and industry and seized hostages. Supplies to Munich broke down. The killing of hostages at the Luitpold Gymnasium on 30 April inflamed opinion against the regime.
bavarian-soviet-republic.e: Government troops and Freikorps units entered Munich on 1-3 May 1919, killing several hundred people, including Landauer. Leviné was executed. The episode pushed Bavarian politics sharply to the right.

beiyang-government.t: The internationally recognised government of the Republic of China based in Beijing, dominated first by Yuan Shikai and then by rival warlord cliques.
beiyang-government.o: Yuan Shikai, commander of the Beiyang Army, the most modern Qing force, negotiated the abdication of the last emperor in 1912 and replaced Sun Yat-sen as president of the new Republic of China, keeping the capital in Beijing. He crushed the Nationalists' Second Revolution of 1913 and governed increasingly as a dictator.
beiyang-government.r: After Yuan's failed attempt to restore the monarchy as the Empire of China (1915-1916) and his death, control of Beijing passed between military cliques: the Anhui clique of Duan Qirui, the Zhili clique of Cao Kun and Wu Peifu, and the Fengtian clique of Zhang Zuolin. Cabinets and presidents changed rapidly, while provinces ruled themselves. China joined the First World War in 1917, and anger at the peace settlement sparked the May Fourth Movement in 1919.
beiyang-government.e: The Nationalist government's Northern Expedition from 1926 defeated the northern warlords. Zhang Zuolin abandoned Beijing in June 1928 and was killed by a Japanese bomb; Beijing was renamed Beiping and the capital moved to Nanjing.

blemmyes.t: Nomadic people of the Eastern Desert, ancestors of the Beja, who raided Roman Egypt and held Lower Nubia in late antiquity.
blemmyes.o: The Blemmyes lived in the desert hills between the Nile and the Red Sea and are generally identified as ancestors of the modern Beja. They appear in Roman sources from the 3rd century CE, raiding Upper Egypt and the trade routes to the Red Sea ports.
blemmyes.r: They were organised in tribes under kings and phylarchs, and in the 5th century held parts of Lower Nubia, with Talmis (Kalabsha) as a centre. In 298 Diocletian withdrew the frontier to Philae and paid subsidies to both the Blemmyes and the Nobadians. The Blemmyes worshipped Isis and had the right to borrow her statue from Philae. Letters written in Greek, such as one from King Phonen, survive at Qasr Ibrim.
blemmyes.e: In the 5th to 6th centuries the Christian kingdom of Nobadia drove them from the Nile valley; King Silko recorded his victories at Kalabsha. The closure of the Philae temple under Justinian around 537 ended their religious tie with Egypt, and their descendants remained in the Eastern Desert.

beylik-of-titteri.t: The smallest of the three provinces of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Médéa by beys who controlled the highlands south of the capital.
beylik-of-titteri.o: The Regency of Algiers organised its territory in the mid-16th century into the provinces of the East, the West and Titteri, with the area around Algiers itself ruled directly. Titteri, created around 1548, covered the Tell Atlas and high plains south of Algiers, with Médéa as its seat.
beylik-of-titteri.r: The bey, appointed by Algiers, collected taxes from tribes and farmers, relying on Janissary garrisons and allied makhzen tribes. Every few years he travelled to Algiers to deliver tribute in person. The province supplied grain, livestock and wool to the capital, and Médéa was a market town with Andalusi and Ottoman influences.
beylik-of-titteri.e: After the French captured Algiers in 1830, the bey Mustapha Boumezrag first submitted and then resisted. French troops occupied Médéa in late 1830, and the beylik was dissolved into French Algeria.

bonampak.t: A small Maya city in the Lacandon forest whose murals give the most vivid surviving picture of a Classic Maya court, battle and ceremony.
bonampak.o: Bonampak, anciently Usiij Witz, was a minor centre near the Lacanjá river in Chiapas. Its lords are attested in the Late Classic from around 600 CE and were for long periods subordinate to their more powerful neighbour Yaxchilan.
bonampak.r: Structure 1 holds three painted rooms, created around 790 under the ruler Yajaw Chan Muwaan. They show the presentation of an heir, a fierce battle, the judgement and torture of captives, and celebrations with dancers and musicians. The murals reveal costume, weapons, music and court hierarchy in rare detail, and show the close involvement of Yaxchilan's royal house.
bonampak.e: The murals were never finished, and Bonampak was abandoned soon after 800 CE. They were revealed to outsiders in 1946 by Lacandon Maya guides, transforming the image of the Maya as peaceful.

bishopric-of-osel-wiek.t: Prince-bishopric of western Estonia and its islands, ruled from Hapsal and Arensburg until its bishop sold it to Denmark in 1559-1560.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.o: After the conquest of Saaremaa in 1227 and of Läänemaa, a bishopric for the islands and the western coast was founded in 1228. Its lands were shared with the Livonian Order, which took parts of Saaremaa and the island of Muhu, while the bishop held most of Läänemaa and western Saaremaa.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.r: The bishops resided first at Lihula, then from the 13th century at Hapsal (Haapsalu), and also built the castle of Arensburg (Kuressaare) on Saaremaa. They governed through German vassals, a cathedral chapter and the diets of Terra Mariana. Repeated Estonian revolts, including the uprising of 1343, shook the islands.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.e: Facing the Livonian War, Bishop Johann von Münchhausen sold the bishopric to Frederick II of Denmark in 1559, and the king passed it to his brother Magnus of Holstein, who arrived in 1560. It became Danish Ösel, and the mainland part fell to Sweden.

berbice.t: A Dutch plantation colony on the Berbice river in Guyana, remembered above all for the great slave uprising of 1763.
berbice.o: In 1627 the Zeeland merchant Abraham van Peere received a charter from the Dutch West India Company to settle the Berbice river. The colony began as a trading post at Fort Nassau upriver and was run as a private patroonship by the van Peere family.
berbice.r: Berbice developed sugar, coffee and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans. After a French raid in 1712, the colony was ransomed and from 1720 run by the Society of Berbice, a company of investors. In 1763 enslaved people led by Coffy rose up, controlled most of the colony for nearly a year and were suppressed only with outside troops. New Amsterdam later became the capital.
berbice.e: Britain occupied Berbice from 1796 and gained it formally in 1814. In 1831 it was merged with Demerara-Essequibo to form British Guiana. Coffy is Guyana's national hero, and 23 February, the start of the uprising, is the country's Republic Day.

bono-state.t: Early Akan kingdom at the forest edge in central Ghana, a gold-trading partner of Mande merchants and forerunner of later Akan states.
bono-state.o: Bono, with its capital at Bono Manso near modern Techiman, is regarded by Akan tradition as one of the earliest Akan kingdoms. It grew where the savanna meets the forest, close to gold-bearing land and to the Mande trading town of Begho. Tradition dates its founding as early as the 13th century, though its chronology is uncertain.
bono-state.r: Bono's kings controlled gold mining and the trade in gold and kola northward to Mande and Hausa traders, receiving cloth, salt and brass. Akan institutions often credited to Bono include the use of gold weights, stools as symbols of office and matrilineal succession. Tradition names Ameyaw Kwaakye as a king under whom gold mining expanded.
bono-state.e: In 1723 the Ashanti Empire under Opoku Ware conquered Bono Manso and destroyed the town. Its people and royal stools were absorbed into the Ashanti system, and the Techiman traditional state claims succession from Bono.

bone-sultanate.t: The most powerful Bugis kingdom of South Sulawesi, whose prince Arung Palakka allied with the Dutch to break the power of Gowa in 1669.
bone-sultanate.o: Bone arose in the 14th century around Watampone on the Gulf of Bone. Its chronicles tell of a tomanurung, a heavenly figure, who agreed to rule with the consent of the local community leaders. By the 16th century it was a rival of Gowa, and in 1582 it formed the Tellumpoccoe alliance with Wajo and Soppeng.
bone-sultanate.r: Bone was ruled by an arumpone, whose power was balanced by a council of seven lords. Gowa conquered it and imposed Islam in 1611. The exiled prince Arung Palakka joined the Dutch East India Company, defeated Gowa in 1666 to 1669, and made Bone the leading state of South Sulawesi.
bone-sultanate.e: Bone resisted the Dutch in the 19th century, and in 1905 they conquered it, exiling its ruler La Pawawoi Karaeng Sigeri. The kingdom was restored under Dutch supervision in 1931 under La Mappanyukki and merged into Indonesia after independence. It is now Bone Regency.

banu-kab-sheikhdom.t: An Arab tribal sheikhdom of the Khuzestan marshes that built canals and a navy and challenged Persians, Ottomans and the East India Company.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.o: The Banu Ka'b, an Arab tribe from southern Iraq, moved into the marshes of the lower Karun in Khuzestan in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, as the Musha'sha weakened. They settled at Qubban and later at Fallahiyeh (modern Shadegan), which became the seat of their sheikhs.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.r: Under Sheikh Salman ibn Sultan (c. 1737 to 1768) the sheikhdom reached its height. He dug canals and built dams for rice and date cultivation, assembled a fleet of armed boats, and resisted campaigns by Karim Khan of the Zand Empire and the Ottoman pasha of Baghdad. In 1765 his ships seized vessels of the East India Company, provoking a British expedition. The Ka'b were Shia and Arabic-speaking.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.e: After Salman's death the sheikhdom fragmented. Its Muhaysin branch developed Mohammerah, and after an Ottoman sack of Mohammerah in 1837 leadership passed to what became the Sheikhdom of Mohammerah.

british-ceylon.t: The British Crown Colony of Ceylon, which unified the island under one administration and built a plantation economy of coffee, tea and rubber.
british-ceylon.o: British forces from the Madras Presidency took the Dutch coastal provinces of Dutch Ceylon in 1795 to 1796, and they became a Crown Colony in 1802. In 1815 the British, exploiting discontent among Kandyan chiefs, took over the Kingdom of Kandy, bringing the whole island under one rule for the first time.
british-ceylon.r: The Colebrooke-Cameron reforms of 1833 centralised administration. Coffee plantations spread in the hills until blight in the 1870s, after which tea, rubber and coconut dominated, worked by Tamil labourers from India. English education created a new elite, and a Buddhist revival led by Anagarika Dharmapala grew. The Donoughmore Constitution of 1931 introduced universal suffrage.
british-ceylon.e: Ceylon contributed to the Allied effort in the Second World War, and the Soulbury Constitution prepared self-government. It gained independence peacefully in 1948 as the Dominion of Ceylon, with D. S. Senanayake as first prime minister.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of Boeotia shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE Thebes was gathering them into a federation, an effort Plataea resisted by allying with Athens. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of Athens at Coronea in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia describes its 5th-century constitution: Boeotia was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with Thebes holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The King's Peace dissolved it in 386 BCE, but Pelopidas and Epaminondas revived it after 379 BCE and defeated Sparta at Leuctra. Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until Rome dissolved it in 171 BCE.

barawa.t: A small Somali port city known for its Islamic scholarship and its own Bantu language, Chimiini, spoken by the Bravanese.
barawa.o: Barawa, or Brava, developed as a coastal trading town on the southern Somali coast in the early second millennium, settled by Somali Tunni clans together with Arab and Swahili-speaking merchants. Arab geographers mention it from around the 12th century, and its people developed the distinct Chimiini dialect of Swahili.
barawa.r: The town was governed by its leading families and religious notables rather than a strong monarchy. It traded hides, ivory and grain from the Shabelle and Jubba valleys, and was famous as a centre of Islamic learning, later linked with the Qadiriyya brotherhood. It resisted the Portuguese, who sacked it in 1506, and was for long tributary to the Ajuran Sultanate.
barawa.e: After Ajuran's decline Barawa came under Omani influence and in 1871 under the Sultanate of Zanzibar. Zanzibar leased the Benadir ports to Italy, and Barawa became part of Italian Somaliland. Its Bravanese community survives, though much reduced by the civil war after 1991.

barony-of-passavant.t: Frankish barony in the Mani held by the marshals of Achaea, whose castle of Passava watched over the unruly Maniots.
barony-of-passavant.o: Around 1220 John of Neuilly, hereditary marshal of the Principality of Achaea, received a fief at the entrance to the Mani peninsula and built a castle there called Passavant, now Passava, near Gytheio. Its purpose was to control the independent-minded population of the Mani and the route into Laconia.
barony-of-passavant.r: The barony was small but held by one of the great officers of the principality, the marshal, who commanded the army. Its lords ruled from the castle over Greek villages, alongside the castle of Grand Magne built by William II of Villehardouin further south.
barony-of-passavant.e: After William II was captured at Pelagonia in 1259, he ceded Mistras, Monemvasia and Grand Magne to Byzantium, and Passavant was lost to the Byzantines soon after, around 1263. The Neuilly heiress Margaret of Passavant later claimed Akova.
