banate-of-leitha.t: State proclaimed by Hungarian irregulars in 1921 to stop the transfer of Burgenland to Austria, whose resistance led to the plebiscite that kept Sopron Hungarian.
banate-of-leitha.o: The peace treaties of Saint-Germain and Trianon assigned German-speaking western Hungary, later called Burgenland, to Austria. When the handover began in August 1921, Hungarian irregulars of the Ragged Guard attacked Austrian gendarmes. On 4 October 1921 their commander, Pál Prónay, proclaimed the independent Banate of Leitha at Oberwart.
banate-of-leitha.r: The banate was a military occupation run by the irregulars, with a provisional administration and its own stamps; the Hungarian government officially disowned it while using it as a bargaining chip. Its population was mostly German-speaking, with Croatian and Hungarian minorities.
banate-of-leitha.e: Under Italian mediation the Venice Protocol of October 1921 agreed a plebiscite in Sopron, and the irregulars withdrew in November. Burgenland passed to Austria, while Sopron voted in December 1921 to stay in Hungary.

british-new-guinea.t: A British protectorate and then colony in southeastern New Guinea, administered for the Australian colonies and handed to Australia as Papua.
british-new-guinea.o: Fearing German expansion, Queensland tried to annex eastern New Guinea in 1883, but Britain disallowed the move. In November 1884 Commodore James Erskine proclaimed a British protectorate over the southeast at Port Moresby, days after Germany had raised its flag over the north, which became German New Guinea. In 1888 the territory was annexed as a crown colony.
british-new-guinea.r: The colony was funded largely by Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. Administrator William MacGregor, from 1888 to 1898, explored the interior, set up government stations, appointed village constables and restricted land sales to Europeans. London Missionary Society workers, including James Chalmers, who was killed in 1901, were influential along the coast. Small gold rushes on Misima and Woodlark Island drew prospectors.
british-new-guinea.e: After federation, Britain transferred the colony to the Commonwealth of Australia, effective under the Papua Act of 1906, when it was renamed the Territory of Papua. MacGregor's network of government stations and village constables remained the basis of Australian administration.
british-new-guinea.la: English, Motu, Papuan and Austronesian languages

banovina-of-croatia.t: Autonomous Croatian province created in 1939 in a late attempt to settle the Serb-Croat conflict within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.o: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia had been divided in 1929 into banovinas that ignored historic borders. With war looming, the regent Prince Paul sought agreement with the Croatian Peasant Party, and the Cvetković-Maček Agreement of 26 August 1939 merged the Sava and Littoral banovinas with parts of Bosnia, Herzegovina, Srem and the Dubrovnik area into one Banovina of Croatia.
banovina-of-croatia.r: The banovina had autonomy over internal administration, education, justice and the economy under a ban, Ivan Šubašić, while Vladko Maček became deputy prime minister of Yugoslavia. A Croatian Sabor was planned but never elected. Serbs in the banovina feared Croatian domination, while the separatist Ustaše rejected any settlement within Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.e: After the Axis invasion of April 1941, the Ustaše proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia on 10 April, ending the banovina. Its borders influenced later debates about Croatia's territory, including the partition of Bosnia discussed in the 1990s.
banovina-of-croatia.re: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam

british-honduras.t: Britain's only colony on the Central American mainland, a mahogany and chicle territory claimed by Guatemala that became independent Belize in 1981.
british-honduras.o: In 1862 Britain formally declared the Belize Settlement a colony, under the name British Honduras, subordinate to the governor of Jamaica. Treaties with Guatemala in 1859 and with Mexico in 1893 fixed its borders, though Guatemala later claimed the whole territory, arguing that Britain had not kept a promise to build a road.
british-honduras.r: The settlers' assembly gave up its powers in 1871, making British Honduras a crown colony, and in 1884 it received its own governor. Mahogany, logwood and later chicle for chewing gum were the main exports, controlled by a few British firms, notably the Belize Estate and Produce Company. The population mixed Creoles, Garifuna, Maya and Mestizo refugees from the Caste War. A hurricane devastated Belize City in 1931.
british-honduras.e: Currency devaluation in 1949 sparked the nationalist People's United Party, led by George Price. Self-government came in 1964, and the colony was renamed Belize in 1973. After Hurricane Hattie, the capital moved to Belmopan in 1970, and Belize became independent on 21 September 1981, with British troops guarding it against Guatemala.

beylik-of-shahrisabz.t: A Kenagas Uzbek beylik around Shahrisabz that defied the emirs of Bukhara until Russia conquered it in 1870.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.o: Shahrisabz, the old city of Kesh and birthplace of Timur, was the stronghold of the Kenagas Uzbek tribe, which long resisted the Manghit Emirate of Bukhara. In the mid-19th century the Kenagas beks under Jura Beg and Baba Beg established effective independence.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.r: The beks ruled a fertile oasis on the Qashqadarya with the neighbouring town of Kitab, fortifying it against Bukhara. They exploited the emirate's conflicts with Russia and Kokand, at times accepting nominal Bukharan overlordship. Little is recorded of their internal government.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.e: In 1870 a Russian force under General Abramov stormed Shahrisabz and handed it to the Emirate of Bukhara, then a Russian protectorate. Jura Beg and Baba Beg fled to Kokand.

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the Pennines and northern England, from the Mersey and Humber to the Tyne. Their name is linked to the goddess Brigantia. By the time of the Roman invasion of 43 they were under the rule of Queen Cartimandua, who made a treaty with Rome and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. Cartimandua handed the fugitive Caratacus to the Romans in 51, and later her divorce from her consort Venutius split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 Venutius drove Cartimandua out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. Petillius Cerialis then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at York. The southern territory became a civitas centred on Isurium Brigantum, Aldborough, in Roman Britain.

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of Iberia, roughly from the Strait of Gibraltar to Almería, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as Malaka, Sexi and Abdera.
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under Hispania Ulterior and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into Baetica.

bodeok.t: A short-lived puppet kingdom set up by Silla to house Goguryeo refugees under a Goguryeo prince after the fall of Pyongyang.
bodeok.o: After Goguryeo fell in 668, Silla backed resistance to Tang China. In 670 it recognised Anseung, a Goguryeo royal, as king of Goguryeo and settled him and his followers at Geummajeo, modern Iksan, in former Baekje territory. In 674 Silla renamed him king of Bodeok.
bodeok.r: Bodeok served Silla's purposes during the war against Tang, giving Goguryeo refugees a figurehead and troops a base. Anseung married into the Silla royal house, and the kingdom sent envoys to Japan. Its autonomy was limited and it remained under close Silla control.
bodeok.e: In 683 Anseung was summoned to Gyeongju, given the Silla royal surname Kim and settled there. When his kinsman Daemun rebelled in 684, Silla crushed the revolt, abolished the kingdom and dispersed its people.

british-java.t: Five-year British rule of Java during the Napoleonic Wars, remembered for Raffles, land-tax reform and the sack of Yogyakarta.
british-java.o: After Napoleon annexed the Netherlands, Britain targeted its colonies. In August 1811 a force from India under Lord Minto and General Samuel Auchmuty landed near Batavia and defeated the Franco-Dutch army of Governor-General Jan Willem Janssens, who capitulated in September. Thomas Stamford Raffles was appointed lieutenant-governor.
british-java.r: Raffles replaced forced deliveries with a land rent assessed on villages, reduced the powers of Javanese regents, and in 1812 stormed the kraton of the Yogyakarta Sultanate, creating Pakualaman. He also attacked the Palembang Sultanate. British officials surveyed Borobudur and Prambanan, and Raffles wrote his History of Java.
british-java.e: The Anglo-Dutch Convention of 1814 returned Java to the Netherlands, and the British handed over in August 1816, when the Dutch East Indies was restored. Some of the land-rent reforms survived, and Raffles went on to found Singapore.

bahurutshe-chiefdom.t: The senior house of the Tswana, whose stone-walled capital Kaditshwene impressed early 19th-century visitors as one of the largest towns in southern Africa.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.o: The Bahurutshe trace their descent from the founding Tswana lineage, from which the Bakwena and other groups later branched. By the 16th century they were settled in the Marico district of the western highveld, where they built aggregated towns with stone-walled cattle enclosures.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns divided into wards, each under a headman, with public assemblies (kgotla) for justice and debate. The economy combined cattle herding, cereal farming and skilled metalworking in iron and copper. When the missionary John Campbell visited Kaditshwene in 1820 he estimated its population at 16,000 and admired its metal crafts and trade.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.e: Kaditshwene was destroyed in the wars of the early 1820s, and the Hurutshe later suffered under Mzilikazi's Ndebele. Reassembled under Moilwa in the Marico valley, they came under the rule of the Transvaal Boer republic after 1852, though Hurutshe communities persist around Zeerust and in Botswana.

balasinor-state.t: A Babi Pathan Nawabi state of central Gujarat, now best known for the dinosaur fossils found on its former lands.
balasinor-state.o: Balasinor was founded around 1758 by a member of the Babi family, the Pathan dynasty that also held Junagadh State and Radhanpur State. It survived the Maratha period by paying tribute to the Gaekwads of Baroda State.
balasinor-state.r: The Nawabs governed a small agricultural territory as part of the Rewa Kantha Agency. Little is recorded about its internal politics. In 1981 large deposits of dinosaur bones and eggs were found at nearby Raiyoli, now a fossil park promoted by members of the former ruling family.
balasinor-state.e: After accession to India Balasinor was merged into Bombay State in 1948 and has been part of Gujarat since 1960; it lies in Mahisagar district.

bhadrawah-state.t: A small hill state in a high valley off the Chenab, contested by Chamba and Jammu before it became part of Jammu and Kashmir.
bhadrawah-state.o: Bhadrawah was ruled by local Rajput chiefs; tradition dates the state to around 1400, but its early history is poorly recorded.
bhadrawah-state.r: Set in a green upland valley, Bhadrawah was for long periods a tributary or dependency of Chamba State. Its people spoke Bhadarwahi, and its Vasuki Nag temple is an important local shrine. Little detail of its government survives.
bhadrawah-state.e: Bhadrawah passed to Gulab Singh of Jammu and became part of Jammu and Kashmir (princely state) in 1846. It is now a town in Doda district.

baro-bhuyans.t: A confederacy of Bengali landholders led by Isa Khan that resisted the Mughal conquest of Bengal for a generation.
baro-bhuyans.o: When the Mughal Empire defeated Daud Khan Karrani in 1576 and ended Afghan rule in Bengal, many landholders in the eastern river delta refused to submit. Known as the Baro-Bhuyans, the twelve landlords, they gathered around Isa Khan, a chief of Afghan and Rajput descent based at Sonargaon.
baro-bhuyans.r: The Bhuyans were Muslim and Hindu zamindars who controlled the waterways of Bhati, the low delta, with fleets of war boats and fortified river posts. They kept their own revenues and alliances, cooperating against Mughal armies. Isa Khan defeated a Mughal fleet in 1584 and fought Man Singh, the Mughal governor.
baro-bhuyans.e: After Isa Khan's death in 1599 his son Musa Khan led the resistance. The Mughal governor Islam Khan moved the capital to Dhaka and defeated Musa Khan by 1611, absorbing eastern Bengal into the Mughal Empire.

barwani-state.t: A Sisodia Rajput state on the Narmada in Nimar, one of the salute states of the Central India Agency.
barwani-state.o: The rulers of Barwani claimed descent from the Sisodia house of Mewar and held lands in the Narmada valley for centuries. The register dates the state to 1650, when the capital was established at Barwani. Its territory had shrunk under Maratha pressure by the 18th century.
barwani-state.r: The Ranas ruled the south bank of the Narmada and the Satpura hills, home to many Bhils. Under British paramountcy it was an eleven-gun salute state in the Bhopawar Agency, with an economy based on cotton and grain. Little is recorded of its rulers beyond these lists.
barwani-state.e: Barwani joined Madhya Bharat in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now a district headquarters.

bida-emirate.t: The Fulani emirate that ruled the Nupe from Bida, a centre of crafts and slave raiding on the middle Niger until the Royal Niger Company's victory in 1897.
bida-emirate.o: In the early 19th century the Fulani cleric Mallam Dendo gained influence in the Nupe Kingdom by exploiting civil wars among its princes, and his sons took control of the country. After further conflicts, Usman Zaki and his brother Masaba emerged as rulers, and around 1856 Bida was founded as the capital of an emirate owing allegiance to the Gwandu Emirate.
bida-emirate.r: Masaba, who ruled from 1859 to 1873, built a strong state with a large army and a network of fiefs held by royal princes. Nupe raided its neighbours heavily for slaves, who worked on royal estates around Bida. The city was famous for its glass beads, brass and silver work and woven cloth, and it traded along the Niger with European merchants.
bida-emirate.e: In January 1897 the Royal Niger Company defeated Emir Abubakar's army outside Bida. British forces occupied the emirate in 1901 within Northern Nigeria, and the Etsu Nupe still reigns at Bida.

bangwato-kingdom.t: The largest Tswana chiefdom, ruled from Shoshong and later Palapye, whose king Khama III helped keep Botswana out of Company rule.
bangwato-kingdom.o: The Bangwato branched off from the Bakwena in the 18th century and settled in what is now central Botswana. After the disruptions of the 1820s they grew under Sekgoma I, with Shoshong as their capital, absorbing many refugees and subject groups.
bangwato-kingdom.r: Chiefs ruled through the kgotla and ward headmen, with cattle as the basis of wealth. Shoshong became a key stop on the missionary and trade road to the north. Khama III, a Christian, became chief in 1875, banned alcohol trading, moved the capital to Palapye in 1889 and promoted the London Missionary Society church.
bangwato-kingdom.e: The Bangwato joined the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. In 1895 Khama travelled to London with other chiefs to resist transfer to the British South Africa Company. His grandson Seretse Khama became Botswana's first president in 1966.

beja-state.t: A tiny Rajput hill state near Kasauli, among the smallest of the Simla Hill States.
beja-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
beja-state.r: Beja consisted of a few villages in the hills south-west of Shimla. It was occupied by the Gurkhas in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
beja-state.e: Beja merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Solan district.

banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.t: The last Almoravid family, which crossed from Majorca to wage a fifty-year war against the Almohads across Ifriqiya and the central Maghreb.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.o: The Banu Ghaniya, descendants of an Almoravid princess, held the Balearic Islands as Banu Ghaniya Majorca after the fall of the Almoravid Empire. In 1184 Ali ibn Ghaniya landed at Bejaia, seized the city from the Almohad Caliphate and opened a war to restore Almoravid rule, recognising the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.r: There was no fixed capital. The Banu Ghaniya fought as a roaming power, allied with Arab tribes such as the Banu Sulaym and, for a time, with Qaraqush. Under Ali's brother Yahya ibn Ghaniya they took Tunis and Mahdia around 1203, devastating towns and countryside across Ifriqiya and Tripolitania.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.e: The Almohad caliph al-Nasir retook Mahdia and Tunis in 1205 to 1206 and installed a Hafsid governor, whose successors kept up the fight. Yahya was driven into the desert and died in the 1230s, ending the movement. The chaos helped the Hafsid Sultanate emerge.

bastarnae.t: Probably Germanic people of the lower Danube and Carpathians who fought for Macedon against Rome and later joined the Goths.
bastarnae.o: The Bastarnae appeared north of the lower Danube around 200 BCE, the first Germanic-speaking people known to Greek and Roman writers, though some ancient authors thought them Celts. One branch, the Peucini, lived on the island of Peuce in the Danube delta.
bastarnae.r: They were a warlike confederation of tribes, valued as mercenaries. Philip V and Perseus of Macedon recruited them against Rome, and the Zarubintsy and Poienești-Lukashevka archaeological cultures are often linked to them. In 62 BCE they defeated Gaius Antonius Hybrida near Histria. In 29 BCE Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated them and killed their king Deldo in single combat.
bastarnae.e: Under the empire they remained a frontier people, joining the Goths and Carpi in 3rd-century raids. Around 280 the emperor Probus settled a large number of Bastarnae in Thrace, after which they disappear as a distinct people.

bajana-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state on the edge of the Little Rann of Kutch, held by a family of Jat Maliks.
bajana-state.o: Bajana lay on the southern edge of the Little Rann of Kutch in the Jhalawad region of Kathiawar. Its rulers were Muslim Jats, who held the estate from around 1700. Its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
bajana-state.r: The ruler governed a dry territory of grazing land and salt flats bordering the Rann. After 1807 Bajana came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency as a minor non-salute state. Few further details are recorded.
bajana-state.e: Bajana merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. Its territory borders the Wild Ass Sanctuary of the Little Rann.

belarusian-peoples-republic.t: The first Belarusian attempt at independence, proclaimed under German occupation in 1918, whose Rada still survives in exile.
belarusian-peoples-republic.o: After the Russian Revolution Belarusian activists formed a Rada in Minsk. While German troops occupied the city, the Rada issued a series of charters, and on 25 March 1918 the Third Constituent Charter declared the Belarusian People's Republic independent of Russia. Jan Sierada became the first chairman of the Rada.
belarusian-peoples-republic.r: The republic never controlled much territory or had an army, as real power lay with the German military. Its government, led by figures such as Raman Skirmunt and later Anton Lutskevich, organised schools in the Belarusian language and sought recognition abroad. It issued passports and sent missions to neighbouring states.
belarusian-peoples-republic.e: When the Germans withdrew in December 1918 the Bolsheviks took Minsk and set up the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia. The Rada went into exile, where it has continued under successive leaders, making it the world's oldest government in exile. 25 March is marked by Belarusian opposition as Freedom Day.

byblos.t: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician port on the Lebanese coast that shipped cedar to Egypt for over two thousand years and gave the Greeks their word for papyrus.
byblos.o: Gubla, as its people called it, is among the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world. By c. 2600 BCE it had become a walled city whose harbour supplied cedar and resin from the Lebanon mountains to the pharaohs of the Old Kingdom of Egypt, receiving gold, linen and papyrus in return.
byblos.r: Kings ruled under the protection of the city's goddess, the Baalat Gebal, whose temple received Egyptian offerings. In the 14th century BCE its king Rib-Hadda sent dozens of the Amarna letters begging Egypt for help. The sarcophagus of King Ahiram bears one of the earliest inscriptions in the Phoenician alphabet, which Byblos helped to shape.
byblos.e: Byblos lost commercial leadership to Tyre and Sidon in the Iron Age and paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire, the Chaldean Empire and the Achaemenid Empire in turn. It submitted peacefully to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE, ending its independent kingship. The town of Jbeil still occupies the site.
